entries.content:
本章脉络

第八章以凯歌结束：没有什么能叫我们与神的爱隔绝。可是一个问题随即出现：神曾经把应许赐给以色列，如今大多数以色列人却拒绝了基督。如果神对以色列的应许都可能落空，我们又凭什么相信罗8:28-39的应许呢？第九至十一章就是回答这个问题。

第九章分四段。保罗的伤痛（1-5节）：他为骨肉之亲「大有忧愁，心里时常伤痛」，甚至愿意自己被咒诅。神的话没有落空（6-13节）：「从以色列生的不都是以色列人」；神的应许从来是照着他的拣选，从以撒和雅各就是这样。神不公平吗？（14-29节）：「断乎没有！」「我要怜悯谁就怜悯谁」；窑匠有权柄处置泥土；神所召的人「不但是从犹太人中，也是从外邦人中」。绊脚石（30-33节）：外邦人因信得了义，以色列人却想靠行为，就跌在那块石头上。

这是罗马书中最难的一章，历代教会对它有许多讨论。读的时候要记得两件事：第一，保罗写这一章，不是带着冷冰冰的逻辑，而是带着眼泪（罗9:2）；第二，这整段论证（九至十一章）的结尾，不是哲学结论，而是敬拜（罗11:33-36）。华人教会在这一章上也有不同立场；但大家都同意：得救全在乎神的怜悯，人仍要为不信负责。读的时候要谦卑，不要拿它来给弟兄姊妹贴标签。

深读 9:1-5 保罗的眼泪

1. 大有忧愁。 「我在基督里说真话，并不谎言，有我良心被圣灵感动，给我作见证：我是大有忧愁，心里时常伤痛。」（罗9:1-2）刚刚说完「得胜有余」（罗8:37），保罗立刻流下眼泪。确信神的爱，并不会叫人对别人的灭亡麻木，反而叫人更为他们伤痛。

2. 愿意被咒诅。 「为我弟兄，我骨肉之亲，就是自己被咒诅，与基督分离，我也愿意。」（罗9:3）这让人想起摩西：以色列人造了金牛犊以后，摩西求神说：「倘或你肯赦免他们的罪……不然，求你从你所写的册上涂抹我的名。」（出32:32）保罗知道这是不可能的（罗8:38-39），可是他的心愿意这样。保罗愿意却不能做的，基督真的做了：他「为我们受了咒诅」（加3:13），在十字架上被离弃，好叫我们永远不与神的爱隔绝。保罗的心，是基督之心的回声。

3. 以色列的特权。 「他们是以色列人；那儿子的名分、荣耀、诸约、律法、礼仪、应许都是他们的。列祖就是他们的祖宗；按肉体说，基督也是从他们出来的。」（罗9:4-5）以色列的特权是真实的，而最大的特权，就是基督按肉体是从他们出来的。

4. 「永远可称颂的神」。 「他是在万有之上，永远可称颂的神。阿们！」（罗9:5）最早的抄本没有标点，所以这句话怎样断句，是编者和译者的判断：有人把后半句读作一句独立的颂赞（「愿那在万有之上的神永远受称颂」）。可是多数解经家都认为，这里是直接称基督为「在万有之上……的神」。这是新约中明确宣告基督神性的经文之一。

要点：保罗确信神的爱，所以为不信的骨肉之亲伤痛；他的心，是那位为我们受咒诅的基督之心的回声。我们认识恩典越深，就越不能对别人的灭亡无动于衷。
深读 9:6-13 不在乎行为，乃在乎召人的主

1. 神的话没有落空。 「这不是说神的话落了空。因为从以色列生的不都是以色列人。」（罗9:6）这是第九至十一章的主题句。神的应许从来不是给每一个按血统作以色列人的，而是给「应许的儿女」（罗9:8）。

2. 以撒与以实玛利。 「惟独『从以撒生的才要称为你的后裔。』」（罗9:7；引创21:12）亚伯拉罕有两个儿子，可是应许是藉着以撒延续的。以撒是一个「应许的儿子」：他的出生本身就是一个神迹（罗4:19）。

3. 雅各与以扫。 有人可能会说：以实玛利的母亲是使女，所以不同。保罗就举出一个更清楚的例子：雅各和以扫是双胞胎，同一个父亲、同一个母亲，「双子还没有生下来，善恶还没有做出来，只因要显明神拣选人的旨意，不在乎人的行为，乃在乎召人的主」（罗9:11）。拣选的根据，不在于人做了什么，甚至不在于人将来会做什么，而是在于神自己。

4. 「雅各是我所爱的；以扫是我所恶的」。（「恶」读wù，憎恶） （罗9:13；引玛1:2-3）这句话常令读者不安。要注意几点：

  • 在希伯来的用语中，「爱」与「恶」的对比，常常表示拣选与不拣选，或「爱这个胜过爱那个」（参创29:30-31，「失宠」原文就是「被恨」；路14:26与太10:37对照）。但玛1:3-4也显明，「恶」包括神对以东的审判；它的意思是不拣选、弃绝，而不是情绪上的怨恨。
  • 玛拉基书讲的是两个民族（以色列和以东）的历史。有解经家因此认为，罗马书第九章讲的是神拣选一个民族，在救恩历史中担当使命，而不是个人的永远得救。
  • 可是也有许多解经家（特别是改革宗传统）指出，保罗在这里的问题正是个人的得救：为什么有些以色列人得救，有些没有（罗9:1-3，27；罗10:1）？而且「不在乎人的行为」这句话，是关乎得救的原则。

无论哪一种理解，保罗的重点都很清楚：神的拣选是出于他的恩典，不在乎人的行为。

要点：神的应许从来不是靠血统或行为，而是靠神自己的拣选。这样，神的话就不会落空，因为它从来不依靠人。
深读 9:14-29 窑匠与泥土

1. 神不公平吗？ 「这样，我们可说什么呢？难道神有什么不公平吗？断乎没有！」（罗9:14）许多（特别是改革宗的）解经家指出，如果拣选是根据人的行为或预见的信心，这个反问就很难出现了。正因为拣选完全在乎神，人才会问：这公平吗？

2. 怜悯的主权。 「因他对摩西说：我要怜悯谁就怜悯谁，要恩待谁就恩待谁。据此看来，这不在乎那定意的，也不在乎那奔跑的，只在乎发怜悯的神。」（罗9:15-16；引出33:19）要留意神的这句话是在什么时候说的：以色列人刚刚造了金牛犊，全民族都配受审判。在那个时候，神宣告自己的名，宣告的正是他的怜悯。保罗讲的拣选，也不是华人所说的「命」或「宿命」：宿命是没有位格、冷漠的定数；圣经的拣选，是一位有位格、满有怜悯的神在基督里施恩，同时要人负责回应（罗9:32）。怜悯，本来就不是人配得的；若是应得的，就不叫怜悯了。

3. 法老。 「因为经上有话向法老说：『我将你兴起来，特要在你身上彰显我的权能，并要使我的名传遍天下。』如此看来，神要怜悯谁就怜悯谁，要叫谁刚硬就叫谁刚硬。」（罗9:17-18；引出9:16）出埃及记在第一场灾难之前，就记载神说「我要使他的心刚硬」（出4:21；出7:3）；接着说法老的心刚硬、法老自己硬着心（出7:13；出8:15，32），然后说「耶和华使法老的心刚硬」（出9:12）。神的主权与人的责任，在圣经中是并存的。神叫人刚硬，从来不是把恶放进一颗无辜的心，而是在一个已经悖逆的罪人身上施行审判，任凭他在自己所选的路上越走越刚硬（参罗1:24-28）；然而保罗在罗9:18把刚硬和怜悯一样，都归在神的主权之下。

4. 「你是谁？」 「这样，你必对我说：『他为什么还指责人呢？有谁抗拒他的旨意呢？』你这个人哪，你是谁，竟敢向神强嘴呢？」（罗9:19-20）保罗没有给一个哲学上的答案，而是提醒我们自己的位置：我们是受造之物，他是创造主。这不是叫人不要思想，而是叫人不要坐在审判官的位置上审判神。

5. 窑匠与器皿。 「窑匠难道没有权柄从一团泥里拿一块做成贵重的器皿，又拿一块做成卑贱的器皿吗？」（罗9:21；参赛29:16；耶18:1-6）自奥古斯丁以来，许多解经家认为，「一团泥」是在亚当里已经堕落的全人类（罗5:12）；也有人认为是指以色列（参耶18章）。无论如何，保罗的重点是窑匠的权柄。神没有冤枉任何人；他向一些人施怜悯，是恩典；他让一些人承受他们自己选择的后果，是公义。要留意罗9:22-23的一个差别：「蒙怜悯」的器皿是神「早预备得荣耀的」，而「可怒」的器皿只说是「预备遭毁灭的」，没有说是谁预备的；而且神对他们也是「多多忍耐宽容」。许多解经家看重这个差别：神是救恩的主动者，而灭亡是罪人应得的。

6. 不是我子民的。 「这器皿就是我们被神所召的，不但是从犹太人中，也是从外邦人中。」（罗9:24）保罗引用何西阿书：「那本来不是我子民的，我要称为『我的子民』。」（罗9:25-26；引何2:23；何1:10）。何西阿原是论到被弃又蒙恢复的北国以色列；保罗看见同样的怜悯原则，如今临到外邦人。神的主权不是叫人绝望的教义：正因为得救在乎神，不在乎人，连那些「本来不是蒙爱的」外邦人，也可以被称为「永生神的儿子」（罗9:26）。

要点：怜悯本来就不是人配得的。神没有亏欠任何人；他向不配的人施怜悯，是何等的恩典。正因为得救只在乎发怜悯的神，连最远的人也有指望。
深读 9:30-33 绊脚石

1. 一个令人惊讶的结果。 「那本来不追求义的外邦人反得了义，就是因信而得的义。但以色列人追求律法的义，反得不着律法的义。」（罗9:30-31）

2. 原因。 「这是什么缘故呢？是因为他们不凭着信心求，只凭着行为求；他们正跌在那绊脚石上。」（罗9:32）这里要留意：保罗在讲完神的主权之后，立刻讲人的责任。以色列人没有得着义，是因为他们自己「不凭着信心求」。神的拣选和人的责任，保罗都同时宣告，并不用一边去否定另一边。

3. 那块石头。 「就如经上所记：我在锡安放一块绊脚的石头，跌人的磐石；信靠他的人必不至于羞愧。」（罗9:33；引赛28:16；赛8:14）这块石头就是基督。想靠自己的人，在他身上绊跌；信靠他的人，却以他为稳固的根基。这块石头今天仍摆在每一个人面前。

要点：神的主权和人的责任，保罗同时宣告。以色列人跌倒，是因为他们想靠行为；同一块石头，对信靠他的人却是磐石。
默想

默想： 「这不在乎那定意的，也不在乎那奔跑的，只在乎发怜悯的神。」我是否在心里暗暗觉得，我能信主，多少是因为我比别人更有悟性、更愿意寻求、更有属灵的胃口？保罗说，我今天能站在恩典中，唯一的原因是神向我发了怜悯；而怜悯，本来就是我不配得的。这样的认识，会叫我在不信的人面前更谦卑，而不是更骄傲。再看保罗：他越确信神的主权，就越为他的骨肉之亲流泪。神的主权在我身上，是否也带出同样的结果：不是冷漠地说「反正神都定好了」，而是更迫切地为我的同胞、我的家乡、我从小一起长大的那群人祷告，也为保罗的骨肉之亲，就是今天的犹太人祷告，因为我知道，连像我这样「本来不是蒙爱的」人，神都能称为「蒙爱的」？如果我读这一章时心里害怕：「万一我不是蒙拣选的呢？」保罗并没有叫我去窥探神隐秘的旨意，而是指给我看那块石头：「信靠他的人必不至于羞愧。」（罗9:33）法老从来没有为自己的刚硬担忧；一颗害怕离神太远、渴望来到基督面前的心，正是神的怜悯在作工的样子。主耶稣说：「到我这里来的，我总不丢弃他。」（约6:37）今天我不必先解开拣选的奥秘，就可以直接投靠他。当我读到这一章难以明白的地方，我能不能先像保罗在罗11:33那样俯伏下来：「深哉，神丰富的智慧和知识！」
entries.content_en:
The Shape of the Chapter

Chapter 8 ended in triumph: nothing can separate us from the love of God. But a question follows at once: God once gave his promises to Israel, yet now most Israelites have rejected Christ. If God's promises to Israel could fail, what grounds do we have to trust the promises of Romans 8:28–39? Chapters 9–11 answer this question.

Chapter 9 has four parts. Paul's anguish (vv. 1–5): he has "great sorrow and unceasing anguish" for his own people, even wishing himself accursed. God's word has not failed (vv. 6–13): "not all who are descended from Israel belong to Israel"; God's promise has always followed his election, from Isaac and Jacob on. Is God unjust? (vv. 14–29): "By no means!" "I will have mercy on whom I have mercy"; the potter has rights over the clay; God's mercy reaches those called "not from the Jews only but also from the Gentiles." The stumbling stone (vv. 30–33): Gentiles attained righteousness by faith, while Israel, pursuing it by works, stumbled over the stone.

This is the hardest chapter in Romans, and the church has debated it through the centuries. Keep two things in mind as you read. First, Paul writes it not with cold logic but with tears (Romans 9:2). Second, this whole argument (chs. 9–11) ends not in a philosophical conclusion but in the worship of Romans 11:33–36. Chinese churches hold different positions on this chapter, but all agree that salvation rests wholly on God's mercy and that people remain responsible for unbelief. Read it humbly, and don't use it to label fellow believers.

Going Deeper: 9:1–5 Paul's Tears

1. Great sorrow. "I am speaking the truth in Christ (I am not lying; my conscience bears me witness in the Holy Spirit) that I have great sorrow and unceasing anguish in my heart" (Romans 9:1–2). Having just said "more than conquerors" (Romans 8:37), Paul is at once in tears. Assurance of God's love does not make a person numb to the lostness of others; quite the opposite.

2. Willing to be accursed. "For I could wish that I myself were accursed and cut off from Christ for the sake of my brothers, my kinsmen according to the flesh" (Romans 9:3). This recalls Moses: after the golden calf, Moses prayed, "But now, if you will forgive their sin, but if not, please blot me out of your book that you have written" (Exod 32:32). Paul knows this is impossible (Romans 8:38–39), yet his heart would be willing. What Paul wished but could not do, Christ actually did: he became "a curse for us" (Gal 3:13), forsaken on the cross so that we would never be separated from God's love. Paul's heart is an echo of Christ's.

3. Israel's privileges. "They are Israelites, and to them belong the adoption, the glory, the covenants, the giving of the law, the worship, and the promises. To them belong the patriarchs, and from their race, according to the flesh, is the Christ" (Romans 9:4–5). Israel's privileges were real, and the greatest of them was that Christ, according to the flesh, came from them.

4. "God over all, blessed forever." "...the Christ, who is God over all, blessed forever. Amen" (Romans 9:5). The earliest manuscripts had no punctuation, so how to divide this sentence is an editorial judgment: some take the last clause as a separate doxology ("God who is over all be blessed forever"). But most interpreters (including the translators of the CUV and ESV) take it as directly calling Christ "God over all." It is one of the New Testament's clear affirmations of Christ's deity.

The point: Because Paul was sure of God's love, he grieved for his unbelieving kinsmen; his heart echoes that of Christ, who became a curse for us. The more deeply we know grace, the less we can be indifferent to the lostness of others.
Going Deeper: 9:6–13 Not Because of Works but Because of His Call

1. God's word has not failed. "But it is not as though the word of God has failed. For not all who are descended from Israel belong to Israel" (Romans 9:6). This is the thesis of chapters 9–11. God's promise was never given to every physical Israelite, but to "the children of the promise" (Romans 9:8).

2. Isaac and Ishmael. "But 'Through Isaac shall your offspring be named'" (Romans 9:7, quoting Gen 21:12). Abraham had two sons, but the promise continued through Isaac. Isaac was a "son of promise": his very birth was God's miracle (Romans 4:19).

3. Jacob and Esau. Someone might say that Ishmael's mother was a servant, so the case is different. So Paul gives a clearer example: Jacob and Esau were twins, with the same father and mother, and "though they were not yet born and had done nothing either good or bad, in order that God's purpose of election might continue, not because of works but because of his call" (Romans 9:11). The ground of election is not what people have done, nor even what they will do, but God himself.

4. "Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated." (Romans 9:13, quoting Mal 1:2–3). This sentence troubles many readers. Note several things:

  • In Hebrew idiom, the contrast of "love" and "hate" often expresses choosing and not choosing, or "loving one more than the other" (cf. Gen 29:30–31; compare Luke 14:26 with Matt 10:37). But Mal 1:3–4 shows that "hated" includes God's judgment on Edom; it means not chosen, rejected, not emotional spite.
  • Malachi speaks of the history of two nations (Israel and Edom). Some interpreters therefore think Romans 9 concerns God's choosing of groups for roles in salvation history rather than the eternal salvation of individuals.
  • Many others (especially in the Reformed tradition) point out that Paul's question here is precisely individual salvation: why some Israelites are saved and others are not (Romans 9:1–3, 27; Romans 10:1). And "not because of works" is a principle of salvation.

On any reading, Paul's point is clear: God's election flows from his grace, not from human works.

The point: God's promise has never rested on bloodline or works, but on God's own election. So God's word cannot fail, because it never depended on us.
Going Deeper: 9:14–29 The Potter and the Clay

1. Is God unjust? "What shall we say then? Is there injustice on God's part? By no means!" (Romans 9:14). Many (especially Reformed) interpreters note that if election rested on works or foreseen faith, this objection would hardly arise. It is precisely because election rests wholly on God that people ask: is this fair?

2. Sovereign mercy. "For he says to Moses, 'I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will have compassion on whom I have compassion.' So then it depends not on human will or exertion, but on God, who has mercy" (Romans 9:15–16, quoting Exod 33:19). Notice when God spoke these words: Israel had just made the golden calf, and the whole nation deserved judgment. At that moment God proclaimed his name, and what he proclaimed was his mercy. Nor is the election Paul speaks of the "fate" or "destiny" of Chinese tradition: fate is impersonal and indifferent; biblical election is a personal, merciful God showing grace in Christ while calling people to respond (Romans 9:32). Mercy means what is not deserved. If it were deserved, it would not be mercy.

3. Pharaoh. "For the Scripture says to Pharaoh, 'For this very purpose I have raised you up, that I might show my power in you, and that my name might be proclaimed in all the earth.' So then he has mercy on whomever he wills, and he hardens whomever he wills" (Romans 9:17–18, quoting Exod 9:16). Before the first plague God announces, "I will harden his heart" (Exod 4:21; Exod 7:3); then Pharaoh's heart is hardened and Pharaoh hardens his own heart (Exod 7:13; Exod 8:15, 32); then "the LORD hardened the heart of Pharaoh" (Exod 9:12). In Scripture, God's sovereignty and human responsibility stand side by side. God's hardening never puts evil into an innocent heart; it is his judicial act on a sinner already in rebellion, giving him over to and confirming him in his chosen way (cf. Romans 1:24–28). Yet in Romans 9:18 Paul places hardening, like mercy, under God's sovereign will.

4. "Who are you?" "You will say to me then, 'Why does he still find fault? For who can resist his will?' But who are you, O man, to answer back to God?" (Romans 9:19–20). Paul gives no philosophical answer; he reminds us of our place: we are creatures, and he is the Creator. This is not a ban on thinking but a ban on sitting as judge over God.

5. The potter and the vessels. "Has the potter no right over the clay, to make out of the same lump one vessel for honored use and another for dishonorable use?" (Romans 9:21; cf. Isa 29:16; Jer 18:1–6). Many interpreters since Augustine take "the same lump" as the human race already fallen in Adam (Romans 5:12); others take it as Israel (cf. Jer 18). Either way, Paul's point is the potter's right. God wrongs no one; to show mercy to some is grace; to let others bear the consequences of their own choices is justice. Note a difference in Romans 9:22–23: the "vessels of mercy" are ones God "has prepared beforehand for glory," while the "vessels of wrath" are simply "prepared for destruction," without saying who prepared them; and God "has endured with much patience vessels of wrath." Many see significance in this difference: God is the active author of salvation, while destruction is what sinners deserve.

6. "Not my people." "Even us whom he has called, not from the Jews only but also from the Gentiles" (Romans 9:24). Paul quotes Hosea: "Those who were not my people I will call 'my people'" (Romans 9:25–26, quoting Hos 2:23; Hos 1:10). Hosea spoke of the northern kingdom of Israel, rejected and then restored; Paul sees the same pattern of mercy now reaching the Gentiles. God's sovereignty is not a doctrine of despair: precisely because salvation depends on God and not on us, even Gentiles who were "not beloved" can be called "sons of the living God" (Romans 9:26).

The point: Mercy means what is not deserved. God owes no one anything; how great a grace it is that he shows mercy to the undeserving. Precisely because salvation depends only on God who has mercy, even those farthest away have hope.
Going Deeper: 9:30–33 The Stumbling Stone

1. A surprising result. "That Gentiles who did not pursue righteousness have attained it, that is, a righteousness that is by faith; but that Israel who pursued a law that would lead to righteousness did not succeed in reaching that law" (Romans 9:30–31).

2. The reason. "Why? Because they did not pursue it by faith, but as if it were based on works. They have stumbled over the stumbling stone" (Romans 9:32). Notice: immediately after speaking of God's sovereignty, Paul speaks of human responsibility. Israel failed to attain righteousness because they themselves "did not pursue it by faith." Paul declares both God's election and human responsibility, without letting either cancel the other.

3. The stone. "As it is written, 'Behold, I am laying in Zion a stone of stumbling, and a rock of offense; and whoever believes in him will not be put to shame'" (Romans 9:33, quoting Isa 28:16; Isa 8:14). The stone is Christ. To those who rely on themselves he is a stumbling stone; to those who trust him he is a firm foundation.

The point: Paul declares God's sovereignty and human responsibility together. Israel stumbled because they relied on works; yet the same stone is a sure rock for all who trust him.
Meditation

Reflect: "It depends not on human will or exertion, but on God, who has mercy." Do I secretly think that I came to faith partly because I was more perceptive, more willing to seek, more spiritually inclined than others? Paul says the only reason I stand in grace today is that God has had mercy on me, and mercy means I didn't deserve it. Knowing this makes me humbler, not prouder, before those who don't believe. Look at Paul too: the surer he was of God's sovereignty, the more he wept for his own people. Does God's sovereignty produce the same in me: not a cold "God has already decided anyway," but more urgent prayer for my own people, my hometown, the community I grew up in, and for Paul's own kinsmen, the Jewish people today, because I know that God can call even someone like me, who was "not beloved," "beloved"? If, reading this chapter, I am afraid, "What if I am not one of the elect?", Paul does not send me to pry into God's hidden decree; he points me to the stone: "whoever believes in him will not be put to shame" (Romans 9:33). Pharaoh never worried about his own hardness; a heart that fears being far from God and longs to come to Christ looks like mercy at work. Jesus said, "whoever comes to me I will never cast out" (John 6:37). Today I can come to him without first solving the mystery of election. When I come to parts of this chapter I find hard to understand, can I first bow down as Paul does in Romans 11:33: "Oh, the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God!"?

entries.verse_text: 你若口里认耶稣为主，心里信神叫他从死里复活，就必得救。
entries.content:
本章脉络

第九章从神的主权讲以色列为什么没有得救；第十章从人的责任来讲同一件事。保罗没有用一边去否定另一边。

本章分三段。热心却不按着真知识（1-4节）：保罗为以色列人祷告，他们「向神有热心」，却「想要立自己的义，就不服神的义了」，因为「律法的总结就是基督」。这道离你不远（5-13节）：出于信心的义不要求人升天下地，只要「口里认耶稣为主，心里信神叫他从死里复活」；而且「凡求告主名的就必得救」，犹太人和希腊人并没有分别。他们听见了吗？（14-21节）：人要求告，先要信；要信，先要听；要听，先要有人传；可是以色列人听见了，却没有都听从。最后神说：「我整天伸手招呼那悖逆顶嘴的百姓。」

深读 10:1-4 两种义

1. 保罗的祷告。 「弟兄们，我心里所愿的，向神所求的，是要以色列人得救。」（罗10:1）保罗讲完了拣选的奥秘，并没有停止为以色列人祷告。相信神主权的人，仍然祷告，而且更迫切地祷告。

2. 热心却不按着真知识。 「我可以证明，他们向神有热心，但不是按着真知识。」（罗10:2）保罗自己就曾经是这样的人：「就热心说，我是逼迫教会的」（腓3:6）。真诚和热心本身不能救人；方向错了，越热心就走得越远。

3. 立自己的义。 「因为不知道神的义，想要立自己的义，就不服神的义了。」（罗10:3）「立」是建造、竖立的意思，像是给自己立一座纪念碑。人的问题，不只是做了坏事，也包括想用好事来建立自己在神面前的地位。这样的人，看起来是在顺服神，其实是不肯「服」神所赐的义，因为接受恩典就要承认自己一无所有。

4. 「律法的总结就是基督」。 「律法的总结就是基督，使凡信他的都得着义。」（罗10:4）「总结」原文 telos，可以指「终结」，也可以指「目标」。解经家有不同的侧重：

  • 有人强调「终结」：律法所代表的时代（摩西之约）在基督里结束了；凡信的人，不再拿律法来「立自己的义」（罗10:3）。其实律法从来就不能使罪人称义（罗3:20）。
  • 有人强调「目标」：律法一直指向基督，在他身上得着成全（参太5:17）。

许多解经家认为两个意思都在其中：基督是律法一直指向的目标；他既来了，律法的时代就结束了，人也不再能拿律法来立自己的义。无论如何，这节经文的重点在下半句：「使凡信他的都得着义。」

要点：真诚和热心本身不能救人。人最深的问题，是想立自己的义，不肯接受神所赐的义；而律法所指向的，正是那位使凡信他的都得着义的基督。
深读 10:5-13 口里承认，心里相信

1. 两种声音。 保罗让两种「义」各自说话。出于律法的义说：「人若行那出于律法的义，就必因此活着。」（罗10:5；引利18:5）利18:5说明律法本身的原则：行了就活（参加3:12）；可是没有一个罪人能这样得生命（罗3:20）。解经家对利18:5原来的语境理解不一，但保罗在这里用它代表「靠行为」的路。

出于信心的义却说：「你不要心里说：谁要升到天上去呢？……谁要下到阴间去呢？」（罗10:6-7）这是引用并改写申30:12-14。申命记30章讲的是以色列被掳归回、神更新他们的心之后的事（申30:1-6；和合本罗30:6作「将你心里和你后裔心里的污秽除掉」，原文是「给你的心行割礼」）；保罗把「过海」改为「下到阴间」，指出这应许在基督的死与复活里应验。摩西原来说的是，神的诫命不是遥不可及的；保罗说，这话在基督身上得着最深的意义：我们不需要上天去把基督领下来，因为他已经道成肉身；也不需要下到阴间把他领上来，因为神已经叫他从死里复活了。

2. 这道离你不远。 「这道离你不远，正在你口里，在你心里。」（罗10:8）福音不要求人去完成一件不可能的任务。基督已经做成了一切，福音就近在咫尺。

3. 「耶稣为主」。 「你若口里认耶稣为主，心里信神叫他从死里复活，就必得救。」（罗10:9）「耶稣是主」是初期教会最早的信仰告白之一（参林前12:3；腓2:11）。当时罗马皇帝常被称为「主」；后来的基督徒更被逼说「凯撒是主」（如《坡旅甲殉道记》）。说「耶稣是主」，就是宣告：我最终只效忠耶稣，连凯撒也不能和他相争。不仅如此，希腊文旧约通常用「主」代替神的圣名「耶和华」；所以称耶稣为主，也是承认他就是耶和华神。

4. 心里与口里。 「因为，人心里相信就可以称义，口里承认就可以得救。」（罗10:10）这不是两个分开的步骤，也不是说要用两种方法得着两样福分（虽然「得救」的范围比「称义」更广，参罗5:9）。这句话与罗10:8所引「口里、心里」对应，是希伯来诗歌式的平行句：里面的信心和外面的承认是同一件事的两面。真正的信心，不会永远藏在心里不说出来。许多华人信徒因为怕家人反对，迟迟不敢公开承认、受洗；他们的承认起初也许软弱、胆怯，但主不轻看这样的信心，而真正的信心迟早要从口里说出来。

5. 凡求告主名的。 「犹太人和希腊人并没有分别，因为众人同有一位主；他也厚待一切求告他的人。因为『凡求告主名的就必得救』。」（罗10:12-13；引珥2:32）约珥书原文的「主」就是「耶和华」；保罗把这句话用在耶稣身上（参罗10:9）。求告耶稣的名，就是求告耶和华的名。这是基督神性的又一个见证。

要点：福音不要求人上天下地去完成不可能的任务，因为基督已经做成了一切。凡口里承认耶稣为主、心里信神叫他复活的人，不分是谁，都必得救。
深读 10:14-21 信道是从听道来的

1. 一条链子。 「然而，人未曾信他，怎能求他呢？未曾听见他，怎能信他呢？没有传道的，怎能听见呢？若没有奉差遣，怎能传道呢？」（罗10:14-15）这是一条倒过来的链子：差遣、传道、听见、相信、求告。神拯救人，是藉着人去传。「未曾听见他」原文也可以译作「未曾听见他说话」，许多解经家认为这个理解更准确：在传道人的话中，人听见的是基督自己的声音。

2. 佳美的脚踪。 「如经上所记：『报福音、传喜信的人，他们的脚踪何等佳美！』」（罗10:15；引赛52:7）以赛亚原来说的是报信的人从远方跑来，宣告被掳的百姓要得释放、神要作王。脚走了长路，满是尘土，在等候消息的人眼中却是「佳美」的。

3. 不是都听从。 「只是人没有都听从福音，因为以赛亚说：『主啊，我们所传的有谁信呢？』」（罗10:16；引赛53:1）这句话出自以赛亚书第四首仆人之歌（赛52:13–53:12）的开头部分。传福音的人不是每一次都会看见果效，连先知也曾这样叹息。

4. 信道从听道来。 「可见，信道是从听道来的，听道是从基督的话来的。」（罗10:17）信心不是靠人自己努力产生的，而是神藉着他的话在人心里创造的。

5. 以色列听见了。 保罗连续引用旧约，说明以色列人不能推说没有听见或不明白：「他们的声音传遍天下」（罗10:18；引诗19:4）；神早就藉摩西说，他要用「那不成子民的」惹动以色列的愤恨（罗10:19；引申32:21）；以赛亚也说，神要被「没有寻找我的」人遇见（罗10:20；引赛65:1）。

6. 伸手招呼的神。 「至于以色列人，他说：『我整天伸手招呼那悖逆顶嘴的百姓。』」（罗10:21；引赛65:2）这是本章最后一句，也是最动人的一句。以色列人「悖逆顶嘴」，神却「整天伸手」。神的主权，从来不是冷冰冰的；他是一位一直向人伸出双手的神。

要点：神拯救人，是藉着人去传他的话，而人在传道中听见的是基督的声音。信心是神藉着他的话创造的，所以传的人只管忠心，不必背负果效的重担。面对悖逆的百姓，神仍然「整天伸手招呼」。
默想

默想： 「他们向神有热心，但不是按着真知识。」我的热心，是建立在神所赐的义上，还是悄悄地在「立自己的义」？这座纪念碑有时是用好事砌成的：我为教会、为真理和人争得面红耳赤，甚至伤了人，心里却觉得这正好证明我比别人更忠心。保罗说，福音不需要我上天下地，因为「这道离你不远」；基督已经做成了，我只需要求告他的名。最后，请再读一次罗10:21：「我整天伸手招呼那悖逆顶嘴的百姓。」在我的生命中，有没有哪一个方面，我一直在对神「顶嘴」？一个我不肯放下的决定、一处我不肯让他进入的地方？神今天仍然向我伸着手，不是要责打我，而是要领我回家。我能不能今天就悔改，放下我的争辩，握住那双为我被钉的手？
entries.content_en:
The Shape of the Chapter

Chapter 9 explained, from God's sovereignty, why Israel has not been saved; chapter 10 explains the same thing from human responsibility. Paul doesn't let one deny the other.

The chapter has three parts. Zeal without knowledge (vv. 1–4): Paul prays for Israel; they have "a zeal for God," but "seeking to establish their own [righteousness], they did not submit to God's righteousness," because "Christ is the end of the law." The word is near you (vv. 5–13): the righteousness of faith doesn't ask anyone to scale heaven or descend to the depths, only to "confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead"; and "everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved," with no distinction between Jew and Greek. Have they not heard? (vv. 14–21): to call, people must believe; to believe, they must hear; to hear, someone must preach; yet Israel heard and did not all obey. Finally God says, "All day long I have held out my hands to a disobedient and contrary people."

Going Deeper: 10:1–4 Two Kinds of Righteousness

1. Paul's prayer. "Brothers, my heart's desire and prayer to God for them is that they may be saved" (Romans 10:1). Having spoken of the mystery of election, Paul has not stopped praying for Israel. Those who believe in God's sovereignty still pray, and pray more urgently.

2. Zeal without knowledge. "I bear them witness that they have a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge" (Romans 10:2). Paul himself had been such a man: "as to zeal, a persecutor of the church" (Phil 3:6). Sincerity and zeal cannot save by themselves; headed in the wrong direction, the more zealous we are, the farther we go.

3. Establishing one's own righteousness. "For, being ignorant of the righteousness that comes from God, and seeking to establish their own, they did not submit to God's righteousness" (Romans 10:3). "Establish" means to set up or erect, like raising a monument to oneself. The human problem is not only doing bad things but trying to use good things to build our standing before God. Such people look as though they are submitting to God, but in fact they refuse to "submit" to the righteousness God gives, because receiving grace means admitting we have nothing.

4. "Christ is the end of the law." "For Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes" (Romans 10:4). "End" (telos) can mean "termination" or "goal." Interpreters place the weight differently:

  • Some stress "termination": the era of the Mosaic law ends in Christ, and for everyone who believes, the law is no longer a means of "establishing one's own righteousness" (Romans 10:3). The law never could justify a sinner (Romans 3:20).
  • Some stress "goal": the law always pointed to Christ and is fulfilled in him (cf. Matt 5:17).

Many think both senses are present: Christ is the goal the law pointed to; now that he has come, the law's era is over, and no one can use the law to establish their own righteousness. Either way, the weight of the verse lies in its second half: "for righteousness to everyone who believes."

The point: Sincerity and zeal cannot save by themselves. Our deepest problem is trying to establish our own righteousness and refusing the righteousness God gives; and the law points to Christ, who gives righteousness to everyone who believes.
Going Deeper: 10:5–13 Confessing with the Mouth, Believing in the Heart

1. Two voices. Paul lets two kinds of "righteousness" speak. The righteousness based on the law says that "the person who does the commandments shall live by them" (Romans 10:5, quoting Lev 18:5). Lev 18:5 states the law's own principle, do and live (cf. Gal 3:12), but no sinner gains life that way (Romans 3:20). Interpreters differ on Lev 18:5 in its original setting, but here Paul uses it for the way of doing. The righteousness based on faith says, "Do not say in your heart, 'Who will ascend into heaven?'... or 'Who will descend into the abyss?'" (Romans 10:6–7). This quotes and adapts Deuteronomy 30:12–14. Deut 30 looks to the time after exile when God circumcises his people's hearts (Deut 30:1–6); Paul changes "beyond the sea" to "the abyss" and sees the promise fulfilled in Christ's death and resurrection. Moses originally said that God's commandment was not out of reach; Paul says the words find their deepest meaning in Christ: we don't need to go up to heaven to bring Christ down, for he has become flesh; nor down into the abyss to bring him up, for God has raised him from the dead.

2. The word is near you. "The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart" (Romans 10:8). The gospel doesn't ask us to accomplish an impossible task. Christ has done it all, so the gospel is close at hand.

3. "Jesus is Lord." "Because, if you confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved" (Romans 10:9). "Jesus is Lord" is one of the church's earliest confessions (cf. 1 Cor 12:3; Phil 2:11). Emperors were commonly called "lord," and later Christians were pressed to say "Caesar is Lord" (e.g. the Martyrdom of Polycarp). To say "Jesus is Lord" was to declare that one's highest allegiance belonged to Jesus. And the Greek Old Testament usually renders God's holy name, "the LORD," as "Lord"; so to call Jesus Lord is also to confess that he is the LORD God.

4. Heart and mouth. "For with the heart one believes and is justified, and with the mouth one confesses and is saved" (Romans 10:10). These are not two separate steps, nor two different blessings gained by two different acts (though "saved" is the broader term, cf. Romans 5:9). The verse mirrors the "mouth... heart" of Romans 10:8 and is Hebrew-style parallelism: inner faith and outward confession are two sides of one thing. Real faith does not stay hidden in the heart forever. Many Chinese believers hesitate to confess Christ openly or be baptized for fear of their families; their first confession may be weak and fearful, but the Lord does not despise such faith, and real faith will in time find its voice.

5. Everyone who calls. "For there is no distinction between Jew and Greek; the same Lord is Lord of all, bestowing his riches on all who call on him. For 'everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved'" (Romans 10:12–13, quoting Joel 2:32). In Joel, "the Lord" is "the LORD"; Paul applies the words to Jesus (cf. Romans 10:9). To call on the name of Jesus is to call on the name of the LORD. This is another witness to Christ's deity.

The point: The gospel doesn't ask us to scale heaven or descend to the depths, for Christ has done it all. Everyone, whoever they are, who confesses with the mouth that Jesus is Lord and believes in the heart that God raised him, will be saved.
Going Deeper: 10:14–21 Faith Comes from Hearing

1. A chain. "But how are they to call on him in whom they have not believed? And how are they to believe in him of whom they have never heard? And how are they to hear without someone preaching? And how are they to preach unless they are sent?" (Romans 10:14–15). The chain runs backward: sending, preaching, hearing, believing, calling. God saves people through people who go and tell. "Of whom they have never heard" can also be read "whom they have never heard," which many commentators prefer: in the preacher's words, people hear the voice of Christ himself.

2. Beautiful feet. "As it is written, 'How beautiful are the feet of those who preach the good news!'" (Romans 10:15, quoting Isa 52:7). Isaiah pictured a messenger running from far away to announce that the exiles would be freed and that God reigns. Feet that had traveled a long road, covered in dust, looked "beautiful" to those waiting for the news.

3. Not all obeyed. "But they have not all obeyed the gospel. For Isaiah says, 'Lord, who has believed what he has heard from us?'" (Romans 10:16, quoting Isa 53:1). These words come near the start of the fourth Servant Song (Isa 52:13–53:12). Those who share the gospel don't always see results; even the prophet sighed like this.

4. Faith comes from hearing. "So faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ" (Romans 10:17). Faith is not produced by our own effort; God creates it in the heart through his word.

5. Israel heard. Paul strings together Old Testament texts to show that Israel cannot plead that they had not heard or understood: "Their voice has gone out to all the earth" (Romans 10:18, quoting Ps 19:4); God had said through Moses that he would make Israel jealous "of those who are not a nation" (Romans 10:19, quoting Deut 32:21); and Isaiah said that God would be found "by those who did not seek me" (Romans 10:20, quoting Isa 65:1).

6. The God who holds out his hands. "But of Israel he says, 'All day long I have held out my hands to a disobedient and contrary people'" (Romans 10:21, quoting Isa 65:2). This is the chapter's last sentence and its most moving. Israel was "disobedient and contrary," yet God held out his hands "all day long." God's sovereignty is never cold; he is a God who keeps stretching out his hands to people.

The point: God saves people through people who carry his word, and in their preaching people hear the voice of Christ. Faith is God's creation through his word, so those who tell can be faithful without carrying the weight of results. Even toward a rebellious people, God holds out his hands "all day long."
Meditation

Reflect: "They have a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge." Is my zeal resting on the righteousness God gives, or am I quietly "establishing my own"? Sometimes the monument is built of good things: I fight hard for my church or for the truth, even wounding people, and secretly take it as proof that I am more faithful than others. Paul says the gospel doesn't require me to scale heaven or descend to the depths, because "the word is near you"; Christ has done it, and I need only call on his name. Finally, read Romans 10:21 again: "All day long I have held out my hands to a disobedient and contrary people." Is there some area of my life where I keep "answering back" to God: a decision I won't give up, a place I won't let him into? God is still holding out his hands to me today, not to strike me but to lead me home. Can I repent today, put down my arguing and take hold of the hands that were nailed for me?

entries.content:
本章脉络

第十章末了，神对以色列说：「我整天伸手招呼那悖逆顶嘴的百姓。」读者自然会问：那么，神是不是已经放弃以色列了？第十一章的回答是：「断乎没有！」

本章分四段。余数（1-10节）：保罗自己就是证据；正如以利亚的时候神留下七千人，「如今也是这样，照着拣选的恩典，还有所留的余数」。失脚不是为了跌倒（11-16节）：以色列的过失，使救恩临到外邦人；而他们将来的「丰满」，更要带来「死而复生」。橄榄树（17-24节）：外邦信徒像野橄榄枝被接上，就不可向被折下来的旧枝子夸口；「神的恩慈和严厉」都要看见。奥秘与颂赞（25-36节）：「以色列人有几分是硬心的，等到外邦人的数目添满了，于是以色列全家都要得救」；「神将众人都圈在不顺服之中，特意要怜恤众人」。最后，保罗不再论证，而是敬拜：「深哉，神丰富的智慧和知识！」

深读 11:1-10 照着拣选的恩典

1. 保罗自己就是证据。 「我且说，神弃绝了他的百姓吗？断乎没有！因为我也是以色列人，亚伯拉罕的后裔，属便雅悯支派的。」（罗11:1）保罗自己就是以色列人，而且曾经逼迫教会；连他这样的人神都救了，可见神并没有弃绝以色列。

2. 以利亚和七千人。 以利亚以为「只剩下我一个人」（罗11:3；引王上19:10），神却说：「我为自己留下七千人，是未曾向巴力屈膝的。」（罗11:4；引王上19:18）在属灵黑暗的时代，信徒常常以为只剩下自己；神却知道他的子民在哪里。

3. 恩典就不是恩典了。 「如今也是这样，照着拣选的恩典，还有所留的余数。既是出于恩典，就不在乎行为；不然，恩典就不是恩典了。」（罗11:5-6）这是全书对恩典最简洁的定义之一：恩典若加上一点点行为，就不再是恩典了。

4. 其余的成了顽梗。 「以色列人所求的，他们没有得着。惟有蒙拣选的人得着了；其余的就成了顽梗不化的。」（罗11:7）保罗引用申29:4、赛29:10和诗69:22-23，说明这种属灵的瞎眼是神的审判：神任凭长久不信的人心里刚硬（罗9:18；参罗10:21）。

要点：在最黑暗的时代，神仍然为自己留下余数，而这余数是「照着拣选的恩典」。恩典若掺杂了行为，就不再是恩典。
深读 11:11-16 失脚不是为了跌倒

1. 断乎不是！ 「我且说，他们失脚是要他们跌倒吗？断乎不是！反倒因他们的过失，救恩便临到外邦人，要激动他们发愤。」（罗11:11）以色列的「失脚」不是故事的结局。神在他们的过失中，把救恩带给了外邦人；而外邦人蒙福，又要叫以色列人「发愤」，就是生出羡慕，回转归向神（参罗10:19；申32:21）。

2. 何况他们的丰满呢？ 「若他们的过失为天下的富足，他们的缺乏为外邦人的富足，何况他们的丰满呢？」（罗11:12）这又是一个「何况」的推论：以色列的失败已经为世界带来了这么大的福气，他们将来的「丰满」，岂不带来更大的福气？「若他们被丢弃，天下就得与神和好，他们被收纳，岂不是死而复生吗？」（罗11:15）

3. 保罗的宣教策略。 「我对你们外邦人说这话；因我是外邦人的使徒，所以敬重我的职分，或者可以激动我骨肉之亲发愤，好救他们一些人。」（罗11:13-14）保罗向外邦人传福音，心里却一直记挂着他的同胞。

4. 圣洁的根。 「所献的新面若是圣洁，全团也就圣洁了；树根若是圣洁，树枝也就圣洁了。」（罗11:16）多数解经家认为，「树根」是指列祖，以及神与亚伯拉罕、以撒、雅各所立的约（参罗11:28）。至于「所献的新面」（背景是民15:17-21），有人认为也是指列祖，也有人认为是指已经信主的犹太余民（罗11:5）。

要点：以色列的失脚不是结局。神在他们的过失中把救恩带给外邦人，又要藉着外邦人蒙福，激动以色列人回转。
深读 11:17-24 野橄榄枝

1. 接在其中。 「若有几根枝子被折下来，你这野橄榄得接在其中，一同得着橄榄根的肥汁。」（罗11:17）神的百姓只有一棵橄榄树（旧约也称以色列为神的橄榄树，耶11:16；何14:6），根是神对列祖的应许。外邦信徒不是另栽了一棵树，而是被接到这棵树上。所以外邦信徒也承受了旧约的应许，亚伯拉罕也成了他们的父（罗4:16）。

2. 不可夸口。 「你就不可向旧枝子夸口；若是夸口，当知道不是你托着根，乃是根托着你。」（罗11:18）这是对外邦教会的严肃警告。教会历史上，外邦基督徒常常轻看、甚至逼迫犹太人，这正是保罗在这里所禁止的。

3. 因信立得住。 「他们因为不信，所以被折下来；你因为信，所以立得住；你不可自高，反要惧怕。」（罗11:20）信心本身就排除了骄傲，因为信心承认一切都是领受的（参罗3:27）。

4. 恩慈和严厉。 「可见，神的恩慈和严厉向那跌倒的人是严厉的，向你是有恩慈的，只要你长久在他的恩慈里；不然，你也要被砍下来。」（罗11:22）这警告首先是对外邦信徒整体说的，也适用于每一个自称信徒的人。不同传统对「被砍下来」有不同的理解：改革宗传统认为，真信徒必蒙保守到底（罗8:30，38-39），这样的警告正是神保守他们的方法之一；那些离开的人，显明他们原本不是真属基督（参约壹罗2:19）。阿民念传统（以及路德宗）多数认为，「只要你长久在他的恩慈里」这个条件要照字面看，真信徒有可能因不信而失落救恩（参来6:4-6）。双方都同意：信心是持续地倚靠神的恩慈，不是做了一次决定就可以不管。

5. 重新接上。 「而且他们若不是长久不信，仍要被接上，因为神能够把他们重新接上。」（罗11:23）神的门从来没有向以色列关上。

要点：外邦信徒是被接上的枝子，不是我们托着根，乃是根托着我们。我们因信立得住，所以不可自高，反要敬畏，长久住在神的恩慈里。
深读 11:25-32 以色列全家都要得救

1. 奥秘。 「弟兄们，我不愿意你们不知道这奥秘（恐怕你们自以为聪明），就是以色列人有几分是硬心的，等到外邦人的数目添满了，于是以色列全家都要得救。」（罗11:25-26）在保罗的用语中，「奥秘」不是神秘难解的事，而是从前隐藏、如今由神启示出来的计划。

2. 「以色列全家」是谁？ 这是本章最多讨论的问题。主要有三种理解：

  • 整个神的子民：加尔文等人认为，「以色列」在这里指由犹太人和外邦人组成的属灵以色列（参罗9:6；加6:16）；他们指出，和合本的「于是」原文是「这样」，讲的是得救的方式，不是时间的先后。
  • 历世历代蒙拣选的犹太人：巴文克、伯克富、亨德里克森等人认为，「以色列全家」指历世历代所有蒙拣选的犹太余民：神所拣选的，一个也不会失落；这与罗11:1-7「余数」的主题和罗11:5的「如今」相连。
  • 将来犹太民族大规模的归信：从清教徒到贺智、慕理，再到近代的克兰菲尔德、穆尔、施莱纳，许多解经家持这个看法；其中既有改革宗学者，也有时代论学者。他们认为，外邦人的数目添满以后，犹太民族整体要回转归向基督。理由是，整章的「以色列」都是指犹太民族，与「外邦人」对比（罗11:25），罗11:25的「等到」也暗示将来会有改变；而且下文说他们「为列祖的缘故是蒙爱的」（罗11:28）。

三种理解都同意：以色列得救，是藉着那位「从锡安出来」的救主（罗11:26），藉着神除去他们罪的约（罗11:27），不是藉着另一条不需要基督的路。（罗11:26-27引用赛59:20-21；赛27:9，参耶31:33-34。保罗大体跟随希腊文旧约，又把「来到锡安」改为「从锡安出来」，可能呼应诗14:7。）

3. 没有后悔的恩赐。 「就着福音说，他们为你们的缘故是仇敌；就着拣选说，他们为列祖的缘故是蒙爱的。因为神的恩赐和选召是没有后悔的。」（罗11:28-29）神向以色列守信，正是我们可以信靠他的根据：他既不收回对以色列的选召，也必不收回对我们的应许（参罗8:28-39）。

4. 怜恤众人。 「因为神将众人都圈在不顺服之中，特意要怜恤众人。」（罗11:32）这句话总结了第一至十一章：外邦人在不顺服之中（第1章），犹太人也在不顺服之中（第2-3章），神这样做，是要让所有的人都只能靠怜恤得救。这不是说每一个人最后都必得救，而是说无论犹太人或外邦人，得救的唯一途径都是怜恤。

要点：神没有弃绝以色列；他的恩赐和选召是没有后悔的。神把众人都圈在不顺服之中，是要叫犹太人和外邦人都只能靠他的怜恤得救。
深读 11:33-36 深哉！

1. 论证变成敬拜。 「深哉，神丰富的智慧和知识！他的判断何其难测！他的踪迹何其难寻！」（罗11:33）保罗讲了十一章的道理，最后不是说「我已经把一切都解释清楚了」，而是说「何其难测」。真正的神学，最终会带人俯伏敬拜。

2. 谁作过他的谋士？ 「谁知道主的心？谁作过他的谋士呢？」（罗11:34；引赛40:13）神的计划不需要人的建议。第九至十一章有许多我们无法完全明白的地方，可是我们可以信靠那位全知的神。

3. 谁先给了他？ 「谁是先给了他，使他后来偿还呢？」（罗11:35；参伯41:11）没有人能叫神欠他的债。我们所有的，都是从他领受的；所以救恩从头到尾都是恩典。

4. 本于他，倚靠他，归于他。 「因为万有都是本于他，倚靠他，归于他。愿荣耀归给他，直到永远。阿们！」（罗11:36）万物从神而来（创造），靠神而存（护理），也要归向神（目的）。人生和历史的意义，不在于人，而在于神的荣耀。

要点：神的计划深不可测，可是他的智慧和怜悯是可以信靠的。没有人能叫神欠他的债；万有都是本于他，倚靠他，归于他。
默想

默想： 「谁是先给了他，使他后来偿还呢？」华人社会很讲「人情」：你帮过我，我就欠你一份情，总要找机会还。我对神是否也有这样的心态？我奉献了、服事了、忍耐了，神就该照顾我的家、保守我的工作，好像他欠我一份人情，像拜神许愿、还愿一样。保罗说，没有人能先给神什么；我手中所有的，连我的信心，都是他先给的，而他最先给我的，是他自己的儿子（罗8:32）。这个真理一面拆掉我的骄傲，一面也释放我：我不需要再跟神算账，好像他欠我；也不需要反过来一辈子拼命「还」神的人情，好像我永远还不清。恩典不是拿来还的，而是拿来领受、享受、感谢的。如果事情没有照我所求的发生，我可以老实地把失望告诉他，却不必把它当成神欠我的账。再想想罗11:18：「不是你托着根，乃是根托着你。」我所信的福音，是从亚伯拉罕、摩西、大卫和众先知一路传下来的，我只是被接上去的野枝子。我对犹太人是否有一些随口而出的成见，比如只把他们看作「会赚钱、很精明」的民族，或者只是「拒绝基督的人」？我能站立得住，只是因为神的恩慈；而同一位恩慈的神，也能把他们重新接上（罗11:23）。今天，我能不能也和保罗一起，把一切想不通的事交托给他，单单说：「愿荣耀归给他，直到永远。阿们！」
entries.content_en:
The Shape of the Chapter

At the end of chapter 10 God said of Israel, "All day long I have held out my hands to a disobedient and contrary people." A reader will naturally ask: has God then given up on Israel? Chapter 11 answers, "By no means!"

The chapter has four parts. The remnant (vv. 1–10): Paul himself is the evidence; as in Elijah's day God kept seven thousand, "so too at the present time there is a remnant, chosen by grace." Stumbling, but not to fall (vv. 11–16): Israel's trespass has brought salvation to the Gentiles, and their future "full inclusion" will mean "life from the dead." The olive tree (vv. 17–24): Gentile believers, grafted in like wild olive shoots, must not boast over the branches broken off; they must see both "the kindness and the severity of God." The mystery and the doxology (vv. 25–36): "a partial hardening has come upon Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles has come in. And in this way all Israel will be saved"; "God has consigned all to disobedience, that he may have mercy on all." At the end Paul stops arguing and worships: "Oh, the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God!"

Going Deeper: 11:1–10 Chosen by Grace

1. Paul himself is the evidence. "I ask, then, has God rejected his people? By no means! For I myself am an Israelite, a descendant of Abraham, a member of the tribe of Benjamin" (Romans 11:1). Paul had persecuted the church; if God could save him, God had not rejected Israel.

2. Elijah and the seven thousand. Elijah thought "I alone am left" (Romans 11:3, quoting 1 Kgs 19:10), but God said, "I have kept for myself seven thousand men who have not bowed the knee to Baal" (Romans 11:4, quoting 1 Kgs 19:18). In dark times believers often think they are the only ones left; God knows where his people are.

3. Otherwise grace would no longer be grace. "So too at the present time there is a remnant, chosen by grace. But if it is by grace, it is no longer on the basis of works; otherwise grace would no longer be grace" (Romans 11:5–6). This is one of the letter's most concise definitions of grace: add even a little bit of works, and grace is no longer grace.

4. The rest were hardened. "What then? Israel failed to obtain what it was seeking. The elect obtained it, but the rest were hardened" (Romans 11:7). Paul quotes Deuteronomy 29:4, Isaiah 29:10 and Psalm 69:22–23 to show that such spiritual blindness is God's judicial hardening (Romans 9:18), which in Scripture falls on persistent unbelief (cf. Romans 10:21).

The point: Even in the darkest times God keeps a remnant for himself, "chosen by grace." Grace mixed with works is no longer grace.
Going Deeper: 11:11–16 Stumbling, but Not to Fall

1. By no means! "So I ask, did they stumble in order that they might fall? By no means! Rather through their trespass salvation has come to the Gentiles, so as to make Israel jealous" (Romans 11:11). Israel's "stumble" is not the end of the story. Through their trespass God brought salvation to the Gentiles, and the Gentiles' blessing is meant to make Israel "jealous," moved with longing to return to God (cf. Romans 10:19; Deut 32:21).

2. How much more their full inclusion! "Now if their trespass means riches for the world, and if their failure means riches for the Gentiles, how much more will their full inclusion mean!" (Romans 11:12). Another "how much more": if Israel's failure has brought such blessing to the world, how much greater blessing will their future "full inclusion" bring? "For if their rejection means the reconciliation of the world, what will their acceptance mean but life from the dead?" (Romans 11:15).

3. Paul's mission strategy. "Now I am speaking to you Gentiles. Inasmuch then as I am an apostle to the Gentiles, I magnify my ministry in order somehow to make my fellow Jews jealous, and thus save some of them" (Romans 11:13–14). Paul preached to Gentiles, yet his heart never stopped carrying his own people.

4. A holy root. "If the dough offered as firstfruits is holy, so is the whole lump, and if the root is holy, so are the branches" (Romans 11:16). Most take "the root" to be the patriarchs, God's covenant with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob (cf. Romans 11:28). "The dough offered as firstfruits" (from Num 15:17–21) is taken by some the same way, and by others as the believing Jewish remnant (Romans 11:5).

The point: Israel's stumbling is not the end. Through their trespass God brought salvation to the Gentiles, and through the Gentiles' blessing he means to move Israel to return.
Going Deeper: 11:17–24 The Wild Olive Shoot

1. Grafted in among them. "But if some of the branches were broken off, and you, although a wild olive shoot, were grafted in among the others and now share in the nourishing root of the olive tree" (Romans 11:17). God's people are one olive tree (the Old Testament calls Israel God's olive tree, Jer 11:16; Hos 14:6), whose root is God's promise to the patriarchs. Gentile believers are not a new tree planted alongside, but shoots grafted into this one. So Gentile believers also inherit the Old Testament promises, and Abraham becomes their father too (Romans 4:16).

2. Do not boast. "Do not be arrogant toward the branches. If you are, remember it is not you who support the root, but the root that supports you" (Romans 11:18). This is a solemn warning to the Gentile church. In church history Gentile Christians have often despised and even persecuted Jews, exactly what Paul forbids here.

3. Standing by faith. "They were broken off because of their unbelief, but you stand fast through faith. So do not become proud, but stand in awe" (Romans 11:20). Faith itself excludes pride, because faith confesses that everything is received (cf. Romans 3:27).

4. Kindness and severity. "Note then the kindness and the severity of God: severity toward those who have fallen, but God's kindness to you, provided you continue in his kindness. Otherwise you too will be cut off" (Romans 11:22). This warning is first addressed to Gentile believers as a group, and it applies to everyone who professes faith. Traditions understand "cut off" differently: the Reformed tradition holds that true believers will be kept to the end (Romans 8:30, 38–39), that such warnings are one of the means by which God keeps them, and that those who fall away show they never truly belonged (cf. 1 John 2:19). Many in the Arminian tradition (and Lutherans) take the condition "provided you continue in his kindness" at face value and hold that a true believer can fall away through unbelief (cf. Heb 6:4–6). Both agree that faith means continuing to rely on God's kindness, not a one-time decision that can then be ignored.

5. Grafted in again. "And even they, if they do not continue in their unbelief, will be grafted in, for God has the power to graft them in again" (Romans 11:23). God's door has never been shut to Israel.

The point: Gentile believers are grafted branches: it is not we who support the root, but the root that supports us. We stand by faith, so we must not be proud but stand in awe, continuing in God's kindness.
Going Deeper: 11:25–32 All Israel Will Be Saved

1. A mystery. "Lest you be wise in your own conceits, I want you to understand this mystery, brothers: a partial hardening has come upon Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles has come in. And in this way all Israel will be saved" (Romans 11:25–26). In Paul's usage, a "mystery" is not something obscure but a plan once hidden and now revealed by God.

2. Who is "all Israel"? This is the chapter's most debated question. There are three main views:

  • The whole people of God: Calvin and others take "Israel" here as the spiritual Israel of Jews and Gentiles together (cf. Romans 9:6; Gal 6:16); they note that "in this way" describes manner, not sequence.
  • The elect Jews of every generation: Herman Bavinck, Louis Berkhof, William Hendriksen and others take "all Israel" as the sum of the remnant through history; God's election will be fully accomplished. This fits the remnant theme of Romans 11:1–7 and the "present time" of Romans 11:5.
  • A future large-scale turning of the Jewish people: many interpreters, from the Puritans and Charles Hodge to John Murray, C. E. B. Cranfield, Douglas Moo and Thomas Schreiner (among them Reformed as well as dispensational scholars; Hodge and Murray were themselves Reformed), think that after the fullness of the Gentiles comes in, the Jewish people as a whole will turn to Christ. They note that "Israel" throughout the chapter means the Jewish people, in contrast to "the Gentiles" (Romans 11:25), that the "until" of Romans 11:25 implies a coming change, and that they are "beloved for the sake of their forefathers" (Romans 11:28).

All three agree that salvation comes through the Deliverer "from Zion" (Romans 11:26, quoting Isa 59:20; Paul follows the Greek OT and has "from Zion" where Isaiah has "to Zion," perhaps echoing Ps 14:7) and through God's covenant to take away sins (Romans 11:27, quoting Isa 59:21; Isa 27:9; cf. Jer 31:33–34), not through some other way that bypasses Christ.

3. Irrevocable gifts. "As regards the gospel, they are enemies of God for your sake. But as regards election, they are beloved for the sake of their forefathers. For the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable" (Romans 11:28–29). God's faithfulness to Israel is the very ground of our confidence in his faithfulness: he will not withdraw his calling of Israel, nor his promises to us (cf. Romans 8:28–39).

4. Mercy on all. "For God has consigned all to disobedience, that he may have mercy on all" (Romans 11:32). This sums up chapters 1–11: Gentiles are in disobedience (ch. 1), and Jews too (chs. 2–3); God has done this so that everyone can be saved only by mercy. This does not mean every person will finally be saved, but that for Jew and Gentile alike, the only way of salvation is mercy.

The point: God has not rejected Israel; his gifts and calling are irrevocable. God has consigned all to disobedience so that Jew and Gentile alike can be saved only by his mercy.
Going Deeper: 11:33–36 Oh, the Depth!

1. Argument becomes worship. "Oh, the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and how inscrutable his ways!" (Romans 11:33). After eleven chapters of argument, Paul doesn't say, "Now I have explained everything," but "how unsearchable." True theology ends in worship.

2. Who has been his counselor? "For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor?" (Romans 11:34, quoting Isa 40:13). God's plan needs no human advice. Much in chapters 9–11 lies beyond our full understanding, but we can trust the all-knowing God.

3. Who has given to him first? "Or who has given a gift to him that he might be repaid?" (Romans 11:35; cf. Job 41:11). No one can put God in their debt. Everything we have, we have received from him; so salvation is grace from first to last.

4. From him, through him, to him. "For from him and through him and to him are all things. To him be glory forever. Amen" (Romans 11:36). All things come from God (creation), are sustained by God (providence) and return to God (purpose). The meaning of life and history lies not in us but in God's glory.

The point: God's plan is beyond our searching out, but his wisdom and mercy can be trusted. No one can put God in their debt; from him and through him and to him are all things.
Meditation

Reflect: "Who has given a gift to him that he might be repaid?" Chinese society runs on renqing, the debt of favors: if you have helped me, I owe you, and I will look for a way to repay. Do I treat God the same way: I have given, served and endured, so God ought to look after my family and protect my job, as though he owed me a favor, like vows made and repaid at a temple? Paul says no one can give God anything first; everything in my hands, even my faith, he gave me first, and the first thing he gave me was his own Son (Romans 8:32). This truth tears down my pride and also sets me free: I don't need to keep accounts with God as though he owed me, nor spend my life trying to "repay" him as though I could never get out of debt. Grace is not something to pay back, but to receive, enjoy and give thanks for. If things have not gone as I asked, I can tell him honestly of my disappointment, without treating it as a debt he owes me. Think too of Romans 11:18: "it is not you who support the root, but the root that supports you." The gospel I believe came down to me through Abraham, Moses, David and the prophets; I am a wild shoot grafted in. Do I carry casual stereotypes about Jewish people, seeing them only as "clever with money," or only as "the people who rejected Christ"? I stand only by God's kindness, and the same kind God is able to graft them in again (Romans 11:23). Today, can I entrust to him everything I cannot work out and say with Paul, "To him be glory forever. Amen"?

verse_parts.text: 所以，弟兄们，我以神的慈悲劝你们，将身体献上，当作活祭，是圣洁的，是神所喜悦的；你们如此事奉乃是理所当然的。不要效法这个世界，只要心意更新而变化，叫你们察验何为神的善良、纯全、可喜悦的旨意。

entries.content:
本章脉络

第十二章开始了罗马书的最后一大段（12–16章）。前十一章讲神为我们做了什么，从这里开始讲我们因此怎样生活。第一个字就是「所以」：基督徒的生活，是对神慈悲的回应。

本章分四段。活祭（1-2节）：「我以神的慈悲劝你们，将身体献上，当作活祭」；「不要效法这个世界，只要心意更新而变化」。一个身体，许多肢体（3-8节）：「不要看自己过于所当看的」；我们在基督里成为一身，各人照所得的恩赐彼此服事。真实的爱（9-16节）：「爱人不可虚假」；彼此亲热、彼此推让，与喜乐的人同乐，与哀哭的人同哭。以善胜恶（17-21节）：「不要以恶报恶」；「伸冤在我，我必报应」；「你不可为恶所胜，反要以善胜恶。」

深读 12:1-2 理所当然的事奉

1. 「所以」与「神的慈悲」。 「所以，弟兄们，我以神的慈悲劝你们，将身体献上，当作活祭。」（罗12:1）「慈悲」原文是复数，可能是沿用希伯来文的说法，表达神怜悯的丰盛（参林后1:3「发慈悲的父」）；而「所以」把它连到前面所讲的一切怜悯：称义、与神相和、儿子的名分、圣灵的内住、不能隔绝的爱（3–8章），一直到罗11:30-32神对犹太人和外邦人的怜恤。保罗劝勉的根据不是惧怕，而是神的慈悲。基督徒的顺服，不是为了换取神的恩典，而是因为已经领受了恩典。

2. 活祭。 旧约的祭物被杀、献在坛上；如今神要的是「活祭」：不是一次性的献上，而是一生每一天把整个人交给他。「身体」表示这献上是具体的：在家里、在工作中、在我们怎样说话、怎样用时间上。

3. 「理所当然的」事奉。 「你们如此事奉乃是理所当然的。」（罗12:1）原文 logikē latreia，有不同的翻译：和合本作「理所当然的」，英文ESV译本作「属灵的敬拜」，也有人译作「合理的事奉」。几个意思可以并存：在神这样的慈悲面前，把自己献上是唯一合理的回应；而且这敬拜不只在礼拜堂里，也在整个生活中。

4. 不要效法，只要变化。 「不要效法这个世界，只要心意更新而变化，叫你们察验何为神的善良、纯全、可喜悦的旨意。」（罗12:2）「效法」是被压进一个模子里；「变化」原文就是福音书描写耶稣「变了形象」的那个字（太17:2），保罗在林后3:18也用这个字描写信徒被神改变。这个世界不断地塑造我们：什么才算成功，什么才值得追求：名校、高薪、买房、让父母有面子。神的方法，是从里面更新我们的心意，叫我们能「察验」，也就是在实际的生活中分辨并认同神的旨意。

要点：基督徒的生活是对神慈悲的回应。在这样的慈悲面前，把整个人献给神，是唯一合理的敬拜；而神从里面更新我们的心意，叫我们不再被这个世界的模子塑造。
深读 12:3-8 一个身体，许多肢体

1. 看得合乎中道。 「我凭着所赐我的恩对你们各人说：不要看自己过于所当看的；要照着神所分给各人信心的大小，看得合乎中道。」（罗12:3）这是心意更新后的第一个表现：对自己有清醒的认识。不是过高，也不是过低，而是照着神所给的来看自己。

2. 一个身子。 「正如我们一个身子上有好些肢体，肢体也不都是一样的用处。我们这许多人，在基督里成为一身，互相联络作肢体，也是如此。」（罗12:4-5）要留意「互相联络作肢体」：我们不只是基督的肢体，也是「互相」的肢体。我需要你，你也需要我。

3. 不同的恩赐。 保罗列出七种恩赐：说预言、作执事、教导、劝化、施舍、治理、怜悯人（罗12:6-8）。这份清单并不完整（参林前12章；弗4:11），里面有看起来很显眼的恩赐，也有不显眼的。每一种都要用心去做：施舍要「诚实」（原文也有「慷慨、单纯」的意思），治理要「殷勤」，怜悯人要「甘心」。

4. 恩赐是恩典。 「按我们所得的恩赐，各有不同。」（罗12:6）「恩赐」（charismata）和「恩典」（charis）在原文同出一个字根。恩赐不是我们的成就，而是神的礼物，所以没有人可以因为恩赐而骄傲，也没有人可以因为自己的恩赐不显眼而自卑。

要点：恩赐是神的恩典，不是我们的成就。在基督的身体里，我们不只属于基督，也彼此相属；没有人可以骄傲，也没有人是多余的。
深读 12:9-16 爱人不可虚假

1. 不可虚假。 「爱人不可虚假。恶，要厌恶；善，要亲近。」（罗12:9）「不可虚假」原文是「没有假冒」（anypokritos），与「假冒为善」同一字根；这个字原指舞台上戴面具演戏的人。爱不能是一场表演。真实的爱也不是不分是非，而是厌恶恶、亲近善。

2. 彼此推让。 「爱弟兄，要彼此亲热；恭敬人，要彼此推让。」（罗12:10）「亲热」原文是家人之间的爱。「彼此推让」原文的意思是「在尊重别人上要争先」：基督徒若要争，就争着尊重别人。华人很懂得「给面子」，也讲究谦让；可是我们给人面子，常常是为了保住自己的面子，或者换取别人将来还我面子，表面推让，心里却在计较排位。保罗说的不是客套，而是真心看重别人，连那些不能回报我们的人也包括在内（参罗12:16）。

3. 火热、喜乐、忍耐、恒切。 「殷勤，不可懒惰；要心里火热，常常服事主。在指望中要喜乐；在患难中要忍耐；祷告要恒切。」（罗12:11-12）「心里火热」原文也可以理解为「在圣灵里火热」。这几句话描写的是一个被神的慈悲点燃的生命。

4. 款待。 「圣徒缺乏，要帮补；客，要一味地款待。」（罗12:13）「款待」原文是「爱陌生人」。在当时，旅行的信徒常常要靠各地的弟兄姊妹接待。

5. 同乐与同哭。 「与喜乐的人要同乐；与哀哭的人要同哭。」（罗12:15）有人说，与哀哭的人同哭比较容易，与喜乐的人同乐反而更难，因为别人的喜乐常常引起我们的嫉妒。真实的爱，能为别人的成功真心高兴，比如亲戚的孩子考上了名校。

6. 俯就卑微的人。 「要彼此同心；不要志气高大，倒要俯就卑微的人。不要自以为聪明。」（罗12:16）在罗马的教会里，有奴隶也有自由人，有穷人也有富人。爱的意思，是愿意和那些在社会上没有地位的人坐在一起。

要点：真实的爱不是一场表演，它的源头是神在基督里先真实地爱了我们。基督既替我们担当了羞辱，又把神儿女的尊荣赐给我们，我们就不必再争着要面子，反而可以争着尊重别人：厌恶恶、亲近善，能与哀哭的人同哭，也能为别人的喜乐真心高兴。
深读 12:17-21 以善胜恶

1. 不要以恶报恶。 「不要以恶报恶；众人以为美的事要留心去做。若是能行，总要尽力与众人和睦。」（罗12:17-18）「若是能行」承认和睦不总是可能的，因为它需要双方；可是我们要尽到自己那一方的力。和睦也不是假装没事，或者让人继续伤害自己。

2. 伸冤在我。 「亲爱的弟兄，不要自己伸冤，宁可让步，听凭主怒；因为经上记着：『主说：「伸冤在我，我必报应。」』」（罗12:19；引申32:35）保罗没有说恶不重要，也没有说公义不会来到。他是说，审判属于神，不属于我们。把伸冤交给神，不是软弱，而是信心：相信神是公义的审判者，任何恶都逃不过他。这里禁止的是私人报复，并没有否定公义的审判：保罗紧接着说，掌权的「是神的用人，是伸冤的，刑罚那作恶的」（罗13:4）。所以，受害的人报警、寻求法律保护，并不违背这节经文。

3. 炭火堆在头上。 「所以，『你的仇敌若饿了，就给他吃，若渴了，就给他喝；因为你这样行就是把炭火堆在他的头上。』」（罗12:20；引箴25:21-22）「把炭火堆在他的头上」，解经家有不同的理解：

  • 多数解经家认为，这是指叫对方感到羞愧、良心受责，以致可能悔改。
  • 也有人认为，这是指若对方始终不悔改，他所受的审判就更重；他们指出旧约中炭火多表示审判（诗140:10），而上一节刚讲到「听凭主怒」。

从下一节「以善胜恶」来看，前一种理解更合乎上下文：我们的目的，是要胜过恶，而不是要胜过人。

4. 以善胜恶。 「你不可为恶所胜，反要以善胜恶。」（罗12:21）以恶报恶，看起来是赢了，其实是被恶胜过了，因为我们变得和那个伤害我们的人一样。基督自己就是这样胜过恶的：「他被骂不还口；受害不说威吓的话，只将自己交托那按公义审判人的主。」（彼前2:23）

要点：把伸冤交给神不是软弱，而是信心。以恶报恶，就是被恶胜过；基督在十字架上以善胜恶，而我们自己就是这样被他的善胜过的；因着他，我们也能走同一条路。
默想

默想： 「所以，弟兄们，我以神的慈悲劝你们。」我对神的顺服，是出于害怕、出于责任，还是出于被他的慈悲感动？请慢慢回想前十一章的「慈悲」：我原是神的仇敌，他却为我舍了儿子；我原该被定罪，他却称我为义；我原是罪的奴仆，他却让我叫他「阿爸」。再想想罗12:19：「不要自己伸冤。」有没有一个人，我心里一直在等他得报应：一个出卖我的同事、一个伤害过我的亲人、一个从来没有道歉的朋友？神没有叫我假装不痛，也没有说这件事不要紧；正因为他是公义的，我才可以把伸冤的事交给他。如果我受过虐待、暴力或犯罪的伤害，向警察、法院、社工或可信任的人求助，寻求保护和公道，并不是「自己伸冤」，而是神所设立的保护（罗13:4）；不报复，也不等于要继续留在危险之中，或者必须马上和一个不安全的人和好。我也可以为那个人祷告，因为我自己就是一个蒙了怜悯的仇敌（罗5:10）。今天，我能不能为那个人做一件小小的善事？如果对方对我并不安全，这件善事不需要靠近他：可以是为他祷告，也可以是放下想要他受苦的念头。不是为了让他知道我有多好，而是因为基督也是这样待我的。
entries.content_en:
The Shape of the Chapter

Chapter 12 begins the final major section of Romans (chs. 12–16). The first eleven chapters told what God has done for us; from here Paul tells how we therefore live. The chapter opens with "therefore": the Christian life is a response to God's mercy.

The chapter has four parts. A living sacrifice (vv. 1–2): "I appeal to you therefore, brothers, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice"; "do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewal of your mind." One body, many members (vv. 3–8): "not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think"; we are one body in Christ, serving one another with the gifts each has received. Genuine love (vv. 9–16): "Let love be genuine"; brotherly affection, outdoing one another in showing honor, rejoicing with those who rejoice and weeping with those who weep. Overcoming evil with good (vv. 17–21): "Repay no one evil for evil"; "Vengeance is mine, I will repay"; "Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good."

Going Deeper: 12:1–2 Spiritual Worship

1. "Therefore" and "the mercies of God." "I appeal to you therefore, brothers, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice" (Romans 12:1). "Mercies" is plural, probably following Hebrew idiom for the fullness of God's compassion (cf. 2 Cor 1:3, "Father of mercies"); and "therefore" ties it to all the mercy Paul has described: justification, peace with God, adoption, the indwelling Spirit, the love nothing can separate us from (chs. 3–8), and God's plan to have mercy on all (Romans 11:30–32). Paul does not ground his appeal in fear but in God's mercies. Christian obedience is not a way to earn grace but a response to grace already received.

2. A living sacrifice. Old Testament sacrifices were killed and placed on the altar; now God wants a "living sacrifice": not a one-time offering, but giving our whole selves to him every day of our lives. "Bodies" makes the offering concrete: at home, at work, in how we speak and spend our time.

3. "Spiritual worship." "Which is your spiritual worship" (Romans 12:1). The phrase logikē latreia is translated in different ways: the ESV has "spiritual worship," the CUV "service that is only right" (理所当然的), and others "reasonable service." The senses can stand together: in the face of such mercy, offering ourselves is the only reasonable response; and this worship is not only in the church building but in the whole of life.

4. Not conformed, but transformed. "Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewal of your mind, that by testing you may discern what is the will of God, what is good and acceptable and perfect" (Romans 12:2). "Conformed" means pressed into a mold; "transformed" is the word the Gospels use for Jesus being "transfigured" (Matt 17:2), and Paul uses it in 2 Cor 3:18 of believers being changed by God. This world constantly shapes us: what counts as success, what is worth pursuing: the top school, the high salary, the apartment, making our parents proud. God's way is to renew our minds from within, so that we can "discern," that is, test and approve God's will in actual life.

The point: The Christian life is a response to God's mercies. In the face of such mercy, offering our whole selves to God is the only reasonable worship; and God renews our minds from within, so that the world's mold no longer shapes us.
Going Deeper: 12:3–8 One Body, Many Members

1. Sober judgment. "For by the grace given to me I say to everyone among you not to think of himself more highly than he ought to think, but to think with sober judgment, each according to the measure of faith that God has assigned" (Romans 12:3). The first sign of a renewed mind is a clear-eyed view of oneself: not too high and not too low, but according to what God has given.

2. One body. "For as in one body we have many members, and the members do not all have the same function, so we, though many, are one body in Christ, and individually members one of another" (Romans 12:4–5). Notice "members one of another": we are not only members of Christ but members of each other. I need you, and you need me.

3. Different gifts. Paul lists seven gifts: prophecy, service, teaching, exhortation, giving, leading and showing mercy (Romans 12:6–8). The list is not complete (cf. 1 Cor 12; Eph 4:11); it includes prominent gifts and quiet ones. Each is to be exercised wholeheartedly: giving "in generosity" (the word also carries the sense of "single-heartedly"), leading "with zeal," acts of mercy "with cheerfulness."

4. Gifts are grace. "Having gifts that differ according to the grace given to us" (Romans 12:6). "Gifts" (charismata) and "grace" (charis) share a root. Gifts are not our achievements but God's presents, so no one may be proud of their gift, and no one need feel inferior because their gift is unnoticed.

The point: Gifts are God's grace, not our achievements. In the body of Christ we belong not only to Christ but to one another; no one may be proud, and no one is superfluous.
Going Deeper: 12:9–16 Let Love Be Genuine

1. Genuine. "Let love be genuine. Abhor what is evil; hold fast to what is good" (Romans 12:9). "Genuine" is literally "unhypocritical"; a "hypocrite" was originally a masked actor on the stage. Love cannot be a performance. Nor is genuine love without moral clarity: it hates evil and clings to good.

2. Outdoing one another in honor. "Love one another with brotherly affection. Outdo one another in showing honor" (Romans 12:10). "Brotherly affection" is the love of family. If Christians compete, it should be to honor others. Chinese culture knows well how to "give face" and to defer politely; but we often give face to protect our own, or to be repaid later, deferring outwardly while still counting rank inwardly. Paul means not etiquette but genuinely valuing others, including those who can never repay us (cf. Romans 12:16).

3. Zeal, joy, patience, prayer. "Do not be slothful in zeal, be fervent in spirit, serve the Lord. Rejoice in hope, be patient in tribulation, be constant in prayer" (Romans 12:11–12). "Fervent in spirit" may also be read "aglow with the Spirit." These lines describe a life set alight by God's mercies.

4. Hospitality. "Contribute to the needs of the saints and seek to show hospitality" (Romans 12:13). "Hospitality" is literally "love of strangers." In those days traveling believers often depended on being welcomed by brothers and sisters in each place.

5. Rejoicing and weeping together. "Rejoice with those who rejoice, weep with those who weep" (Romans 12:15). It has been said that weeping with those who weep is easier than rejoicing with those who rejoice, because others' joy often stirs our envy. Genuine love can be truly glad at someone else's success, such as a relative's child getting into a top school.

6. Associating with the lowly. "Live in harmony with one another. Do not be haughty, but associate with the lowly. Never be conceited" (Romans 12:16). The Roman church included slaves and free, poor and rich. Love means being willing to sit with those who have no standing in society.

The point: Genuine love is no performance; its source is the genuine love God first showed us in Christ. Because Christ bore our shame and gave us the honor of God's children, we no longer need to compete for face but can compete to honor others; such love hates evil and clings to good, weeps with those who weep, and is truly glad at others' joy.
Going Deeper: 12:17–21 Overcoming Evil with Good

1. Repay no one evil for evil. "Repay no one evil for evil, but give thought to do what is honorable in the sight of all. If possible, so far as it depends on you, live peaceably with all" (Romans 12:17–18). "If possible" admits that peace is not always achievable, because it takes two; but we must do our part. Peace does not mean pretending nothing happened, or letting someone keep harming us.

2. Vengeance is mine. "Beloved, never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God, for it is written, 'Vengeance is mine, I will repay, says the Lord'" (Romans 12:19, quoting Deut 32:35). Paul doesn't say that evil doesn't matter, or that justice will never come. He says judgment belongs to God, not to us. Leaving vengeance to God is not weakness but faith: trusting that God is the righteous judge and that no evil will escape him. What is forbidden is personal revenge, not the just judgment carried out by lawful authority: Paul goes on to call the governing authority "the servant of God, an avenger who carries out God's wrath on the wrongdoer" (Romans 13:4). So a victim who reports a crime or seeks legal protection is not disobeying this verse.

3. Burning coals on his head. "To the contrary, 'if your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him something to drink; for by so doing you will heap burning coals on his head'" (Romans 12:20, quoting Prov 25:21–22). Interpreters understand "burning coals" in different ways:

  • Most take it to mean causing the enemy to feel shame and a stricken conscience, which may lead to repentance.
  • Others take it to mean that if the enemy never repents, his judgment will be heavier, noting that coals in the OT usually signal judgment (Ps 140:10) and that v. 19 has just spoken of God's wrath.

The next verse, "overcome evil with good," makes the first reading fit the context better: our aim is to overcome evil, not to beat a person.

4. Overcoming evil with good. "Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good" (Romans 12:21). Repaying evil for evil looks like winning, but in fact it means being overcome by evil, because we become like the one who hurt us. This is how Christ himself overcame evil: "When he was reviled, he did not revile in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten, but continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly" (1 Pet 2:23).

The point: Leaving vengeance to God is not weakness but faith. To repay evil with evil is to be overcome by evil; Christ overcame evil with good at the cross, and we ourselves were won over by that goodness; because of him, we can walk the same road.
Meditation

Reflect: "I appeal to you therefore, brothers, by the mercies of God." Does my obedience to God come from fear, from duty, or from being moved by his mercy? Slowly recall the "mercies" of chapters 1–11: I was God's enemy, yet he gave his Son for me; I deserved condemnation, yet he justified me; I was a slave of sin, yet he lets me call him "Abba." Think too of Romans 12:19: "never avenge yourselves." Is there someone I have been quietly waiting to see get what they deserve: a coworker who betrayed me, a relative who hurt me, a friend who never apologized? God does not ask me to pretend it didn't hurt or didn't matter; it is because he is just that I can hand vengeance over to him. If I have suffered abuse, violence or crime, going to the police, the courts, a social worker or someone I trust for protection and justice is not "avenging myself"; it is part of the protection God has provided (Romans 13:4). Refusing revenge does not mean staying in danger, or reconciling at once with someone who is not safe. And I can pray for that person, because I myself am an enemy who received mercy (Romans 5:10). Today, can I do one small good thing for that person? If they are not safe for me, that good thing need not bring me near them: it may be a prayer for them, or letting go of my wish to see them suffer. Not to show them how good I am, but because this is how Christ has treated me.

entries.verse_text: 总要披戴主耶稣基督，不要为肉体安排，去放纵私欲。
entries.content:
本章脉络

第十二章末了，保罗说不要自己伸冤，「伸冤在我」。第十三章接着说：在这个世代，神设立在上掌权的，作他伸冤的工具。

本章分三段。顺服掌权的（1-7节）：「没有权柄不是出于神的」；掌权的「是神的用人」，所以信徒要顺服、纳粮上税，「当恭敬的，恭敬他」。爱的债（8-10节）：「凡事都不可亏欠人，惟有彼此相爱要常以为亏欠」，因为「爱就完全了律法」。黑夜已深，白昼将近（11-14节）：「我们得救，现今比初信的时候更近了」，所以要「脱去暗昧的行为，带上光明的兵器」，「总要披戴主耶稣基督」。

这三段劝勉彼此相连，背景是同一个时刻：基督已经来了，又将要再来。信徒活在「白昼将近」的时候，所以用新的眼光看政府、看邻舍、看自己的身体。

深读 13:1-7 掌权的是神的用人

1. 权柄出于神。 「在上有权柄的，人人当顺服他，因为没有权柄不是出于神的。凡掌权的都是神所命的。」（罗13:1）这是旧约一贯的教导：神「废王，立王」（但2:21）。保罗写这封信时，罗马皇帝是尼禄，就是后来逼迫基督徒的那位皇帝；可是在他执政初期（主后54-59年左右），罗马的治理相对平稳。保罗说，就连不信神的政府，权柄也是出于神。

2. 掌权者的职分。 「作官的原不是叫行善的惧怕，乃是叫作恶的惧怕……因为他是神的用人，是与你有益的。你若作恶，却当惧怕，因为他不是空空地佩剑；他是神的用人，是伸冤的，刑罚那作恶的。」（罗13:3-4）保罗在这里描写的是政府应有的职分：赏善罚恶，维护公义和秩序。罗12:19说「不要自己伸冤……听凭主怒」，罗13:4就用了同样的字（「伸冤」「怒」）：掌权者是「伸冤的」。神在今世藉着掌权者，部分地、暂时地施行公义；完全的伸冤要等到神审判的日子（罗2:5）。

3. 顺服的界限。 保罗的命令是普遍的，可是圣经其他地方清楚地表明，顺服掌权者有一个界限：当人的命令与神的命令冲突时，「顺从神，不顺从人，是应当的」（徒5:29；参但3章；6章）。保罗自己也曾因传福音被关进监里。福音派对这一段的理解大致有两种侧重：

  • 有人强调，这段经文是在描写神设立政府的目的；一个政府若颠倒善恶、逼迫行善的人，就背离了神所赋予的职分，信徒可以用合法的方式抗议，甚至在必要时不服从（这是加尔文《基督教要义》4.20.31-32以来改革宗的一个传统）。
  • 也有人强调，保罗（和彼得，彼前2:13-17）是在一个不认识神、后来更逼迫教会的帝国中写这些话的，所以信徒的基本态度应当是顺服和尊重，除非被要求直接违背神的命令。

两种理解都同意：顺服掌权者不是无条件的，而信徒最高的效忠属于耶稣（罗10:9）。无论身处哪一种政治环境，信徒都要为在上掌权的祷告（提前2:1-2），因为他们和我们一样，要站在神的台前；也要预备为顺从神付上代价。

4. 因为良心。 「所以，你们必须顺服，不但是因为刑罚，也是因为良心。」（罗13:5）基督徒遵守法律，不只是怕被罚，也是因为在神面前有清洁的良心。

5. 凡人所当得的。 「你们纳粮，也为这个缘故……凡人所当得的，就给他。当得粮的，给他纳粮；当得税的，给他上税；当惧怕的，惧怕他；当恭敬的，恭敬他。」（罗13:6-7）这让人想起耶稣的话：「凯撒的物当归给凯撒，神的物当归给神。」（太22:21）诚实纳税，尊重在上位的人，即使我们不喜欢他们，也是对神的顺服。

要点：掌权的是神的用人，为要赏善罚恶。信徒因着良心顺服、纳税、尊重在上位的人；可是我们最高的效忠属于耶稣，当人的命令与神的命令冲突时，顺从神是应当的。
深读 13:8-10 永远还不完的债

1. 只有一样债。 「凡事都不可亏欠人，惟有彼此相爱要常以为亏欠，因为爱人的就完全了律法。」（罗13:8）罗13:7讲「凡人所当得的，就给他」：税、粮、惧怕、恭敬，这些都可以付清。可是有一样债是永远付不清的，就是爱。我们爱了别人一次，并不因此就和他两清了。这不是我们还欠神的人情、一辈子还不完（参罗11:35）；而是基督的爱不断地流到我们身上，又从我们流向邻舍，这爱没有用完的一天。

2. 爱完全了律法。 「像那不可奸淫，不可杀人，不可偷盗，不可贪婪，或有别的诫命，都包在爱人如己这一句话之内了。」（罗13:9；引利19:18）这与耶稣的教导完全一致（太22:39-40）。爱不是取代了诫命，而是诫命的总纲：诫命告诉我们，爱在具体的生活中是什么样子。

3. 爱不加害与人。 「爱是不加害与人的，所以爱就完全了律法。」（罗13:10）十诫后半部都在保护邻舍的婚姻、生命、财物和名誉。爱邻舍，就是不伤害他，并且积极地为他谋求益处。

要点：税可以付清，爱的债却永远付不清。爱不是取代诫命，而是诫命的总纲；爱邻舍，就是不伤害他，并且为他的益处着想。
深读 13:11-14 白昼将近

1. 认识时候。 「再者，你们晓得，现今就是该趁早睡醒的时候；因为我们得救，现今比初信的时候更近了。」（罗13:11）这里的「得救」，是指基督再来时救恩的完成（参罗8:23）。每过一天，我们离那一天就更近一天。

2. 黑夜已深，白昼将近。 「黑夜已深，白昼将近。我们就当脱去暗昧的行为，带上光明的兵器。」（罗13:12）这个世代是「黑夜」，可是黑夜已经快过去了；基督的复活已经让第一道曙光照进来。信徒是「属乎白昼」的人（参帖前5:5-8），所以要像早上起床的人一样，脱下睡衣，穿上白天的衣服。

3. 三对罪。 「行事为人要端正，好像行在白昼。不可荒宴醉酒；不可好色邪荡；不可争竞嫉妒。」（罗13:13）保罗把「争竞嫉妒」和醉酒、淫乱放在一起。在教会里，我们常常认为醉酒和淫乱是大罪，争竞和嫉妒却只是个性问题；保罗却把它们一起列为「暗昧的行为」。

4. 披戴主耶稣基督。 「总要披戴主耶稣基督，不要为肉体安排，去放纵私欲。」（罗13:14）「披戴」是穿衣服的意思。信徒在受洗时已经「披戴基督」了（加3:27）；现在要每天重新穿上他：在思想、言语、行为上，活出基督的样式。奥古斯丁说，他在米兰的花园里读到罗13:13-14这两节，「顿觉有一道恬静的光射到心中，溃散了阴霾笼罩的疑阵」（《忏悔录》8.12，周士良译），从此归信基督。

5. 不要为肉体安排。 「安排」原文 pronoia，是预先筹划、准备的意思。罪很少是突然临到的，常常是我们事先给它留了门：去某个地方、留着某些东西、跟某些人来往。保罗说，不要给肉体预备机会。

要点：黑夜已深，白昼将近。信徒活在基督再来之前的清晨，所以要脱去暗昧的行为，每天披戴主耶稣基督，不给肉体留下机会。
默想

默想： 「当得税的，给他上税；……当恭敬的，恭敬他。」我在报税、开发票、填报销单这些小事上，是否诚实？我是否觉得「大家都这样」，或者「政府不好，所以少交一点也没关系」？保罗写这段话时，罗马皇帝是尼禄。我能诚实，不是因为掌权的人都值得尊敬，而是因为耶稣才是我的主（罗10:9）：我的生计在他手里，不靠多报一张发票、少交一点税；我也不必惧怕掌权的，或讨好他们。若我在这些事上已经不诚实，基督的血也能洗净我的良心；我可以在他面前认罪，在能弥补的地方去弥补，不必再一直藏着。再想想罗13:14：「总要披戴主耶稣基督。」披戴，不是靠自己织一件新衣服，而是穿上神为我预备好的衣服。我今天的「白天的衣服」不是我自己的义，而是基督自己。我能不能在今天早上，像穿衣服一样，有意识地对主说：「主啊，今天我要披戴你」？然后看看：有没有一扇我常常为肉体留着的门，今天需要关上？
entries.content_en:
The Shape of the Chapter

At the end of chapter 12 Paul said not to avenge ourselves: "Vengeance is mine." Chapter 13 goes on to speak of an instrument of justice God has appointed in this age: the governing authorities.

The chapter has three parts. Submitting to the authorities (vv. 1–7): "there is no authority except from God"; the ruler "is God's servant," so believers submit, pay taxes and give "honor to whom honor is owed." The debt of love (vv. 8–10): "Owe no one anything, except to love each other," for "love is the fulfilling of the law." The night is far gone; the day is at hand (vv. 11–14): "salvation is nearer to us now than when we first believed," so "let us cast off the works of darkness and put on the armor of light," and "put on the Lord Jesus Christ."

These three sections are not unrelated pieces of advice. They all belong to a particular moment: Christ has come and will come again. Believers live as "the day is at hand," so they see government, neighbors and their own bodies with new eyes.

Going Deeper: 13:1–7 The Ruler Is God's Servant

1. Authority comes from God. "Let every person be subject to the governing authorities. For there is no authority except from God, and those that exist have been instituted by God" (Romans 13:1). This is the consistent teaching of the Old Testament: God "removes kings and sets up kings" (Dan 2:21). When Paul wrote, the emperor was Nero, who later persecuted Christians; but in the early years of his reign (c. AD 54–59) Roman government was relatively stable. Paul says that even an unbelieving government holds its authority from God.

2. The ruler's task. "For rulers are not a terror to good conduct, but to bad... for he is God's servant for your good. But if you do wrong, be afraid, for he does not bear the sword in vain. For he is the servant of God, an avenger who carries out God's wrath on the wrongdoer" (Romans 13:3–4). Paul describes what government is meant to do: reward good and punish evil, upholding justice and order. Romans 12:19 said "never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God"; Romans 13:4 picks up the same words ("avenger," "wrath"). In this age God carries out a partial, provisional justice through governing authorities; full vengeance awaits the day of God's judgment (Romans 2:5).

3. The limits of submission. Paul's command is general, but Scripture elsewhere makes clear that submission to authorities has a limit: when human commands conflict with God's, "we must obey God rather than men" (Acts 5:29; cf. Dan 3; 6). Paul himself was imprisoned for preaching the gospel. Evangelicals read this passage with two main emphases:

  • Some stress that the passage describes God's purpose for government; a government that turns good and evil upside down and persecutes those who do good has abandoned its God-given task, and believers may protest by lawful means, and if necessary refuse to comply (a strand of Reformed thought going back to Calvin, Institutes 4.20.31–32).
  • Others stress that Paul (and Peter, 1 Pet 2:13–17) wrote within a pagan empire that would later persecute the church, so the believer's basic posture should be submission and respect, except when commanded to disobey God directly.

Both agree that submission to authorities is not unconditional, and that the believer's highest allegiance belongs to Jesus (Romans 10:9). In any political setting, believers pray for those in authority (1 Tim 2:1–2), for they too will stand before God, and are ready to pay the cost of obeying God.

4. For the sake of conscience. "Therefore one must be in subjection, not only to avoid God's wrath but also for the sake of conscience" (Romans 13:5). Christians keep the law not only for fear of punishment but to keep a clean conscience before God.

5. Pay to all what is owed. "For the same reason you also pay taxes... Pay to all what is owed to them: taxes to whom taxes are owed, revenue to whom revenue is owed, respect to whom respect is owed, honor to whom honor is owed" (Romans 13:6–7). This recalls Jesus' words: "Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's" (Matt 22:21). Paying taxes honestly and respecting those in authority, even when we don't like them, is obedience to God.

The point: Rulers are God's servants to reward good and punish evil. Believers submit for conscience' sake, pay taxes and respect those in authority; but our highest allegiance belongs to Jesus, and when human commands conflict with God's, we must obey God.
Going Deeper: 13:8–10 A Debt Never Paid Off

1. Only one debt. "Owe no one anything, except to love each other, for the one who loves another has fulfilled the law" (Romans 13:8). Verse 7 said "pay to all what is owed": taxes, revenue, respect, honor, all of which can be paid in full. But one debt can never be paid off: love. Loving someone once doesn't make us "even." This is not a favor we are anxiously repaying to God (cf. Romans 11:35); it is that Christ's love keeps flowing to us and through us to our neighbor, and it never runs out.

2. Love fulfills the law. "The commandments, 'You shall not commit adultery, You shall not murder, You shall not steal, You shall not covet,' and any other commandment, are summed up in this word: 'You shall love your neighbor as yourself'" (Romans 13:9, quoting Lev 19:18). This matches Jesus' teaching exactly (Matt 22:39–40). Love does not replace the commandments but sums them up: the commandments show what love looks like in concrete life.

3. Love does no wrong. "Love does no wrong to a neighbor; therefore love is the fulfilling of the law" (Romans 13:10). The second-table commandments protect our neighbor, for example their marriage, life, property and good name. To love a neighbor is not to harm them, and actively to seek their good.

The point: Taxes can be paid in full, but the debt of love never can. Love does not replace the commandments but sums them up; to love a neighbor is not to harm them and to seek their good.
Going Deeper: 13:11–14 The Day Is at Hand

1. Knowing the time. "Besides this you know the time, that the hour has come for you to wake from sleep. For salvation is nearer to us now than when we first believed" (Romans 13:11). "Salvation" here means its completion when Christ returns (cf. Romans 8:23). Every day brings us one day nearer.

2. The night is far gone. "The night is far gone; the day is at hand. So then let us cast off the works of darkness and put on the armor of light" (Romans 13:12). This age is "night," but the night is nearly over; Christ's resurrection has already let in the first light of dawn. Believers are "children of the day" (cf. 1 Thess 5:5–8), so, like people getting up in the morning, they take off their nightclothes and put on the clothes of the day.

3. Three pairs of sins. "Let us walk properly as in the daytime, not in orgies and drunkenness, not in sexual immorality and sensuality, not in quarreling and jealousy" (Romans 13:13). Paul puts "quarreling and jealousy" alongside drunkenness and sexual sin. In church we often treat drunkenness and immorality as serious sins, and quarreling and jealousy as mere personality issues; Paul lists them all together as "works of darkness."

4. Put on the Lord Jesus Christ. "But put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh, to gratify its desires" (Romans 13:14). "Put on" is the language of clothing. Believers "put on Christ" at their baptism (Gal 3:27); now they are to put him on afresh every day, living out his likeness in thought, word and deed. Augustine tells how he read these two verses (Romans 13:13–14) in a garden in Milan: "it was as though a light of certainty had been poured into my heart, and all the darkness of doubt vanished away" (Confessions 8.12.29, translated from the Latin), and he turned to Christ.

5. Make no provision for the flesh. "Provision" (pronoia) means planning or preparing in advance. Sin rarely ambushes us out of nowhere; usually we have left a door open for it beforehand: going to a certain place, keeping certain things, keeping certain company. Paul says: don't make arrangements for the flesh.

The point: The night is far gone; the day is at hand. Believers live in the early morning before Christ's return, so they cast off the works of darkness, put on the Lord Jesus Christ each day, and leave no opening for the flesh.
Meditation

Reflect: "Taxes to whom taxes are owed... honor to whom honor is owed." In small things like filing taxes, issuing receipts or submitting expense claims, am I honest? Do I tell myself "everyone does it," or "the government is bad, so paying a bit less doesn't matter"? When Paul wrote this, the emperor was Nero. I can be honest, not because every ruler deserves respect, but because Jesus is my Lord (Romans 10:9): my livelihood is in his hands, not in one more padded receipt or a little less tax, and I need neither fear rulers nor flatter them. If I have already been dishonest in these things, Christ's blood can cleanse my conscience too; I can confess it to him, put right what I can, and stop hiding it. Think too of Romans 13:14: "put on the Lord Jesus Christ." Putting on is not weaving a new garment myself, but wearing one God has prepared for me. My "clothes for the day" are not my own righteousness but Christ himself. This morning, can I deliberately say to the Lord, as I would while dressing, "Lord, today I put you on"? And then look: is there a door I keep open for the flesh that I need to close today?
