entries.title: 表明主的死，直等到他来：敬拜中的蒙头与圣餐
entries.title_en: Proclaiming the Lord's Death Until He Comes: Head Coverings and the Lord's Supper

verse_parts.text: 你们每逢吃这饼，喝这杯，是表明主的死，直等到他来。

entries.verse_text: 你们每逢吃这饼，喝这杯，是表明主的死，直等到他来。
entries.content:
本章脉络

第十一章开始讨论教会聚会中的问题（11-14章）。这一章分两段。蒙头（2-16节）：男人祷告或讲道时不可蒙头，女人祷告或讲道时要蒙头；保罗从「头」的次序、创造和「本性」来说明，又说「照主的安排，女也不是无男，男也不是无女」。主的晚餐（17-34节）：哥林多人聚会时「各人先吃自己的饭，甚至这个饥饿，那个酒醉」；保罗提醒他们，主耶稣在被卖的那一夜怎样设立圣餐，并且要他们「自己省察，然后吃这饼、喝这杯」。

两段都关乎聚会中的次序与彼此尊重，第二段更是全章的重心：「你们每逢吃这饼，喝这杯，是表明主的死，直等到他来。」（林前11:26）

深读 11:2-16 蒙头

1. 「头」是什么意思？ 「我愿意你们知道，基督是各人的头；男人是女人的头；神是基督的头。」（林前11:3）「头」原文是 kephalē。这个词在这里的意思，学者有不同的看法： - 权柄：许多主张男女角色有别的学者（常称为互补派，如古德恩、派博）认为，「头」是指带领和权柄，正如弗5:23所说：「丈夫是妻子的头，如同基督是教会的头」。 - 源头：许多主张男女在教会和家庭中角色平等的学者（常称为平等派，如戈登·费依）认为，「头」是指生命的来源，与林前11:8「女人乃是由男人而出」相呼应。 - 也有学者（如锡塞尔顿）认为，「头」是指显要、代表的地位。

「神是基督的头」也要小心理解：子与父同等（腓2:6；约10:30），子是在救赎的工作上甘心顺服（参林前15:28），不表示子在本质上次于父（子的顺服在什么范围内，福音派中也有讨论，但都承认子与父同质同等）。无论哪一种看法，「头」都不是丈夫辖制、苛待妻子的理由；圣经所说的「头」，是像基督那样「为教会舍己」（弗5:25）。家庭暴力是罪，包括身体、言语、经济上的控制，以及借用顺服的经文来压制人。受害人可以寻求保护，包括报警（罗13:4），也不必留在危险之中。教会不可劝受害人回到施暴者身边「更加顺服」，也不可为了「家丑不可外扬」而遮掩。

2. 女人也祷告、讲道。 「凡女人祷告或是讲道，若不蒙着头，就羞辱自己的头。」（林前11:5）「讲道」原文是说预言。大多数解经家认为，这节经文表明，在哥林多教会的聚会中，女人也公开祷告、说预言，保罗并没有禁止，只是要她们蒙头。所以，林前14:34「妇女在会中要闭口不言」不能理解为女人在聚会中完全不可以开口；那节经文的意思，要到第十四章再讨论。

3. 蒙头是什么？ 在当时的希腊罗马社会，已婚的妇女在公开场合用外衣或头巾盖头，表示端庄，也表示自己是有夫之妇；不蒙头，可能被看作轻浮，甚至羞辱丈夫。也有学者认为，保罗说的不是头巾，而是把长发盘起来，不披头散发（参林前11:15「这头发是给她作盖头的」）。林前11:10「因此，女人为天使的缘故，应当在头上有服权柄的记号」是全段最难解的一句：有人认为天使在敬拜中观看，有人认为是指天使维护神所定的次序，也有人认为「权柄」是指女人有权柄祷告、说预言的记号。

4. 今天还要蒙头吗？ 华人教会在这件事上有不同的做法： - 弟兄会传统、倪柝声所建立的聚会处（及后来的地方教会）、真耶稣教会，以及中国大陆不少家庭教会，认为蒙头的吩咐建基于神在创造中定下的次序（林前11:8-9），不只是当时的风俗，所以姊妹至今在聚会中仍然蒙头。 - 大多数福音派教会认为，保罗所教导的原则是长久的，但蒙头这个表达方式与当时的文化有关。至于这原则是什么，主张男女角色有别的人认为是尊重神所定的带领次序，主张角色平等的人认为是在敬拜中不要让性别的分别被抹去、不要叫人羞愧。

不论我们采用哪一种做法，都要记住保罗在林前11:11-12所说的：「然而照主的安排，女也不是无男，男也不是无女。因为女人原是由男人而出，男人也是由女人而出；但万有都是出乎神。」在主里，男女彼此需要，同是照着神的形象造的（创1:27），也「一同承受生命之恩」（彼前3:7）。

要点：在敬拜中，男女都要以尊荣神、尊重彼此的方式来到神面前。在主里，男女彼此需要，都蒙基督舍己的爱，一同承受生命之恩。
深读 11:17-22 不是吃主的晚餐

1. 聚会反而招损。 「我现今吩咐你们的话，不是称赞你们；因为你们聚会不是受益，乃是招损。」（林前11:17）早期教会的圣餐，是在一顿共同的饭中举行的（犹大书12节称这样的聚餐为爱席），通常在较富裕的信徒家中。

2. 「这个饥饿，那个酒醉」。 「你们聚会的时候，算不得吃主的晚餐；因为吃的时候，各人先吃自己的饭，甚至这个饥饿，那个酒醉。」（林前11:20-21）许多学者（如泰森〔Gerd Theissen〕、墨菲-奥康纳〔Jerome Murphy-O'Connor〕）根据当时房屋的格局推想：富有的信徒可以早到，在主人家的餐厅里吃好的；奴隶和穷人做完工才赶来，只能在外面的庭院里吃剩下的，甚至没有东西吃。也有学者（如温特）认为，问题不在先到后到，而在富人独自享用自己的饭，所以林前11:33也可以理解为彼此接待。无论哪一种，都是把社会上的阶级分别，带进了主的晚餐。

3. 藐视神的教会。 「你们要吃喝，难道没有家吗？还是藐视神的教会，叫那没有的羞愧呢？」（林前11:22）保罗说，这样做不只是不礼貌，而是「藐视神的教会」。今天的华人教会也可能有这样的分别：主日崇拜后的午餐，说粤语的和说普通话的、中文堂和英文堂的、新移民和老移民、有钱的和没钱的，各坐各的桌子；有些弟兄姊妹总是一个人吃饭，没有人理会。

要点：主的晚餐记念基督为他所有的子民舍身；在主的桌前，不论贫富，都是蒙恩的罪人，没有高低之分。
深读 11:23-26 主耶稣被卖的那一夜

1. 从主领受的。 「我当日传给你们的，原是从主领受的，就是主耶稣被卖的那一夜，拿起饼来，祝谢了，就擘开，说：『这是我的身体，为你们舍的，你们应当如此行，为的是记念我。』」（林前11:23-24）「领受」和「传给」是传递传统的用语（参林前15:3）。哥林多前书大约写于主后五十三至五十五年，所以这段经文是新约中最早的圣餐记载之一，与路22:19-20非常接近。

2. 新约的血。 「饭后，也照样拿起杯来，说：『这杯是用我的血所立的新约，你们每逢喝的时候，要如此行，为的是记念我。』」（林前11:25）按照对观福音的记载，耶稣设立圣餐，是在逾越节的晚餐中（参林前5:7「我们逾越节的羔羊基督已经被杀献祭了」）。他的血成就了耶利米所应许的新约：神要赦免他百姓的罪孽，不再记念他们的罪恶（耶31:31-34）。

3. 记念与宣告。 「你们每逢吃这饼，喝这杯，是表明主的死，直等到他来。」（林前11:26）「记念」不只是心里想起一件过去的事，更像以色列人守逾越节，是像以色列人守逾越节那样，在神面前重新领受：那次拯救，今天仍然是为我们成就的。每一次领圣餐，教会都在「表明」（宣告）主的死；而且是「直等到他来」，圣餐也叫我们盼望主再来。主说：「直到我在我父的国里同你们喝新的那日子」（太26:29）；每一次领圣餐，都是在预尝那一天的筵席。

要点：圣餐回头看十字架，看见基督「为你们舍的」身体；也向前看，「直等到他来」。
深读 11:27-34 自己省察

1. 「不按理」。 「所以，无论何人，不按理吃主的饼，喝主的杯，就是干犯主的身、主的血了。」（林前11:27）「不按理」原文是一个副词（anaxiōs），讲的是吃喝的方式，不是吃的人配不配。在上下文中，「不按理」就是17-22节所说的：自己吃饱喝醉，却藐视饥饿的弟兄。没有一个人配领圣餐；圣餐正是为那些知道自己不配、却投靠基督的罪人预备的。

2. 「分辨是主的身体」。 「人应当自己省察，然后吃这饼、喝这杯。因为人吃喝，若不分辨是主的身体，就是吃喝自己的罪了。」（林前11:28-29）「主的身体」有几种理解：有人认为是指在饼和杯中所记念的基督的身体；也有人（如戈登·费依）认为是指教会，就是基督的身体（参林前10:17；林前12:27）；不分辨主的身体，就是不顾念弟兄姊妹。也有人认为两方面都包括在内。要注意：保罗说「自己省察，然后吃」，省察的目的是来领受，不是叫人离开主的桌子。

3. 被主惩治。 「因此，在你们中间有好些软弱的与患病的，死的也不少。我们若是先分辨自己，就不至于受审。我们受审的时候，乃是被主惩治，免得我们和世人一同定罪。」（林前11:30-32）保罗说，哥林多教会中有些疾病和死亡，是神的管教。但这不表示每一次生病都是因为某个罪（参约9:3）。而且保罗特别说，这是「惩治」（管教），目的是「免得我们和世人一同定罪」：神管教的，正是他所爱的儿女（来12:6）。

4. 软弱的良心。 有些敏感的信徒，因为想起自己的罪，就不敢领圣餐，一次又一次地让饼和杯从面前经过。据说十九世纪苏格兰的约翰·邓肯〔John Duncan〕牧师，看见一位妇人流着泪推开杯，就对她说：「拿去吧，这是为罪人预备的。」若我们为罪忧伤，又投靠基督，主的桌子正是为我们预备的。真正需要停下来的，是那些继续活在明知的罪中、不肯悔改，或者正在与弟兄姊妹结怨、却不愿和好的人（参太5:23-24）。这不是要受害人与伤害他的人和好；饶恕不等于恢复关系，也不等于让伤害人的人恢复职分或再接近受害人与孩子，受害人不必回到危险之中。就算是前面那样的人，主的呼召也是悔改，然后来到桌前。

5. 彼此等待。 「所以我弟兄们，你们聚会吃的时候，要彼此等待。」（林前11:33）这是这一段实际的结论：不要自己先吃，要等那些晚来的、穷乏的弟兄姊妹。

要点：没有人配领圣餐；圣餐是为投靠基督的罪人预备的。省察自己，是为了悔改、和好，然后来到主的桌前。
默想

默想： 「这是我的身体，为你们舍的。」也许我已经有好几次在圣餐时，让饼和杯从面前经过，因为我想起这个星期发的脾气、看过不该看的东西、心里的怨恨和冷淡，觉得自己不配。保罗说：「人应当自己省察，然后吃这饼、喝这杯。」省察不是要我把自己关在门外，而是要我带着这一切来到十字架前：承认自己的罪；能与我得罪过的人和好的，就去和好，一时还不能的，也交托在主面前；然后伸手领受。主耶稣在被卖的那一夜设立这饼和杯，那一夜他的门徒都要离开他，彼得也要三次不认他；他却仍然说：「这是我的身体，为你们舍的。」我能领圣餐，从来不是因为我这个星期表现得够好，而是因为他的身体已经为我舍了，他的血已经为我流了。也许我自己就是主日午餐时常常一个人吃饭的人，没有人招呼我；主却在他的桌前亲自说：「我很愿意在受害以先和你们吃这逾越节的筵席」（路22:15）。领受了这样的恩典，我也就能邀请另一位一个人吃饭的弟兄姊妹，与我同坐一桌。下一次领圣餐的时候，我能不能不再把手缩回来，而是相信：这桌筵席是主亲自为我摆设的，有一天，我还要在父的国里与他同喝新的（太26:29）？
entries.content_en:
The Shape of the Chapter

Chapter 11 begins Paul's treatment of problems in the church's gatherings (chs. 11–14). The chapter has two parts. Head coverings (vv. 2–16): a man should not cover his head when he prays or prophesies, and a woman should cover hers; Paul argues from the order of "heads," from creation and from "nature," and adds that "in the Lord woman is not independent of man nor man of woman." The Lord's Supper (vv. 17–34): when the Corinthians gather, "each one goes ahead with his own meal. One goes hungry, another gets drunk"; Paul reminds them how the Lord Jesus instituted the Supper on the night he was betrayed, and tells them to "examine himself, then, and so eat of the bread and drink of the cup."

Both parts concern order and mutual honor in worship, and the second is the heart of the chapter: "For as often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you proclaim the Lord's death until he comes" (1 Corinthians 11:26).

Going Deeper: 11:2–16 Head Coverings

1. What does "head" mean? "But I want you to understand that the head of every man is Christ, the head of a wife is her husband, and the head of Christ is God" (1 Corinthians 11:3). "Head" translates kephalē. Scholars differ on its meaning here: - Authority: many complementarian scholars (e.g. Wayne Grudem, John Piper) take "head" to mean leadership and authority, as in Ephesians 5:23: "the husband is the head of the wife even as Christ is the head of the church." - Source: many egalitarian scholars (e.g. Gordon Fee) take "head" to mean source of life, echoing 1 Corinthians 11:8, "woman from man." - Others (e.g. Anthony Thiselton) take it to mean prominence or representative standing.

"The head of Christ is God" must also be read with care: the Son is equal with the Father (Phil 2:6; John 10:30), and the Son's submission is a willing submission in the work of redemption (cf. 1 Corinthians 15:28); it does not mean the Son is lesser in nature than the Father (evangelicals debate how far this submission extends, but all confess the Son is of one being and equal with the Father). On any view, "head" gives no husband a reason to dominate or mistreat his wife; the headship Scripture describes is that of Christ, who "gave himself up for her" (Eph 5:25). Domestic violence is sin, including physical, verbal and financial control and the use of "submission" texts to dominate. Victims may seek protection, including from the police (Rom 13:4), and need not remain in danger. The church must not urge a victim to go back and "submit more," nor hide abuse to save face.

2. Women also prayed and prophesied. "But every wife who prays or prophesies with her head uncovered dishonors her head" (1 Corinthians 11:5). Most interpreters take this verse to show that in the Corinthian gatherings women also prayed and prophesied publicly; Paul doesn't forbid it, only asks that they be covered. So 1 Corinthians 14:34, "the women should keep silent in the churches," cannot mean that women may never speak at all in the gathering; what that verse means will be taken up in chapter 14.

3. What was the covering? In Greco-Roman society married women covered their heads in public with a mantle or veil, signaling modesty and marriage; to go uncovered could be seen as loose, even as shaming one's husband. Some scholars think Paul has in mind not a veil but long hair bound up rather than let down (cf. 1 Corinthians 11:15, "her hair is given to her for a covering"). Verse 10, "a wife ought to have a symbol of authority on her head, because of the angels," is the hardest sentence in the passage: some think angels watch over worship, some that they guard God's order, and some that the "authority" is the woman's own authority to pray and prophesy.

4. Should women cover their heads today? Chinese churches differ in practice: - Some churches (e.g. in the Brethren tradition, the assemblies and local churches associated with Watchman Nee, the True Jesus Church and many house churches in mainland China) hold that the head covering itself is grounded in the order God set at creation (1 Corinthians 11:8–9), not merely in custom, so sisters still cover their heads in the gathering. - Most evangelical churches hold that the principle Paul teaches is lasting, but that the head covering as its expression belongs to that culture. As to what the principle is, complementarians see honoring the order of leadership God has set, while egalitarians see not erasing the distinction between the sexes in worship, and not bringing shame.

Whatever our practice, we must remember 1 Corinthians 11:11–12: "Nevertheless, in the Lord woman is not independent of man nor man of woman; for as woman was made from man, so man is now born of woman. And all things are from God." In the Lord, men and women need each other; both are made in the image of God (Gen 1:27) and are "heirs with you of the grace of life" (1 Pet 3:7).

The point: In worship, men and women alike come before God in ways that honor him and one another. In the Lord, men and women need each other; both are loved by the self-giving Christ and share together in the grace of life.
Going Deeper: 11:17–22 Not the Lord's Supper

1. Gatherings that do harm. "But in the following instructions I do not commend you, because when you come together it is not for the better but for the worse" (1 Corinthians 11:17). The early church held the Lord's Supper within a shared meal (Jude 12 calls such meals "love feasts"), usually in the home of a wealthier believer.

2. "One goes hungry, another gets drunk." "When you come together, it is not the Lord's supper that you eat. For in eating, each one goes ahead with his own meal. One goes hungry, another gets drunk" (1 Corinthians 11:20–21). Many scholars (e.g. Gerd Theissen, Jerome Murphy-O'Connor), reconstructing from the layout of houses at the time, think the wealthy could arrive early and eat well in the host's dining room, while slaves and the poor came after work, ate leftovers in the courtyard, or had nothing at all. Others (e.g. Bruce Winter) think the problem was not timing but the rich devouring their own meals, so that 1 Corinthians 11:33 can mean "receive one another." Either way, society's class divisions were being carried into the Lord's Supper.

3. Despising the church of God. "What! Do you not have houses to eat and drink in? Or do you despise the church of God and humiliate those who have nothing?" (1 Corinthians 11:22). Paul says this isn't just bad manners; it is "despising the church of God." Chinese churches today can have such divisions too: at lunch after Sunday worship, Cantonese and Mandarin speakers, Chinese and English congregations, new and old immigrants, the well-off and the poor each sit at their own tables, and some brothers and sisters always eat alone with no one noticing.

The point: The Lord's Supper remembers Christ, who gave his body for all his people; at the Lord's table, rich and poor alike are sinners shown grace, with no high or low.
Going Deeper: 11:23–26 The Night He Was Betrayed

1. Received from the Lord. "For I received from the Lord what I also delivered to you, that the Lord Jesus on the night when he was betrayed took bread, and when he had given thanks, he broke it, and said, 'This is my body which is for you. Do this in remembrance of me'" (1 Corinthians 11:23–24). "Received" and "delivered" are the language of handing on tradition (cf. 1 Corinthians 15:3). First Corinthians was written around AD 53–55, so this is among the earliest written accounts of the Lord's Supper in the New Testament, very close to Luke 22:19–20.

2. The blood of the new covenant. "In the same way also he took the cup, after supper, saying, 'This cup is the new covenant in my blood. Do this, as often as you drink it, in remembrance of me'" (1 Corinthians 11:25). According to the Synoptic Gospels, Jesus instituted the Supper at the Passover meal (cf. 1 Corinthians 5:7, "Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed"). His blood brings in the new covenant Jeremiah promised, in which God forgives his people's iniquity and remembers their sin no more (Jer 31:31–34).

3. Remembering and proclaiming. "For as often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you proclaim the Lord's death until he comes" (1 Corinthians 11:26). "Remembrance" is not merely calling a past event to mind; like Israel keeping the Passover, it is acknowledging before God that his saving act still concerns us now. Each time the church takes the Supper it "proclaims" the Lord's death, "until he comes," so the Supper is also a hope for the Lord's return. He said, "until that day when I drink it new with you in my Father's kingdom" (Matt 26:29); every Supper is a foretaste of that feast.

The point: The Supper looks back to the cross and sees Christ's body "which is for you"; it looks forward, "until he comes."
Going Deeper: 11:27–34 Let a Person Examine Himself

1. "In an unworthy manner." "Whoever, therefore, eats the bread or drinks the cup of the Lord in an unworthy manner will be guilty of profaning the body and blood of the Lord" (1 Corinthians 11:27). "In an unworthy manner" translates an adverb (anaxiōs); it describes the way one eats, not whether the person is worthy. In context it is what verses 17–22 describe: eating and drinking one's fill while despising the hungry brother. No one is "worthy" of the Supper; it is set for sinners who know they are unworthy and take refuge in Christ.

2. "Discerning the body." "Let a person examine himself, then, and so eat of the bread and drink of the cup. For anyone who eats and drinks without discerning the body eats and drinks judgment on himself" (1 Corinthians 11:28–29). "The body" is read in several ways: some take it as Christ's body remembered in the bread and cup; others (e.g. Gordon Fee) as the church, the body of Christ (cf. 1 Corinthians 10:17; 1 Corinthians 12:27), so that the fault is disregarding one's brothers and sisters; others think both are included. Notice that Paul says "examine himself, then, and so eat": the purpose of self-examination is to come and receive, not to keep people away from the table.

3. Disciplined by the Lord. "That is why many of you are weak and ill, and some have died. But if we judged ourselves truly, we would not be judged. But when we are judged by the Lord, we are disciplined so that we may not be condemned along with the world" (1 Corinthians 11:30–32). Paul says some illness and death in the Corinthian church was God's discipline. That does not mean every illness is caused by a particular sin (cf. John 9:3). And Paul stresses that this is discipline, "so that we may not be condemned along with the world": God disciplines the children he loves (Heb 12:6).

4. Tender consciences. Some sensitive believers, remembering their sins, dare not take the Supper and let the bread and cup pass them by time after time. It is said that a nineteenth-century Scottish minister, John Duncan, saw a woman in tears push the cup away, and said to her, "Take it, woman; it's for sinners." If we grieve over our sin and take refuge in Christ, the Lord's table is set precisely for us. Those who truly need to pause are those who persist in known sin without repentance, or who hold a grudge against a brother or sister and refuse to be reconciled (cf. Matt 5:23–24; this does not require a victim to reconcile with someone who has harmed them: forgiveness is not the same as restored relationship, nor does it restore an offender's office or access to victims and children, and no one need return to danger); and even to them the Lord's call is to repent, and then come to the table.

5. Wait for one another. "So then, my brothers, when you come together to eat, wait for one another" (1 Corinthians 11:33). This is the practical conclusion: don't eat first; wait for the brothers and sisters who come late and have little.

The point: No one is worthy of the Supper; it is set for sinners who take refuge in Christ. We examine ourselves in order to repent and be reconciled, and then to come to the Lord's table.
Meditation

Reflect: "This is my body which is for you." Perhaps several times at the Lord's Supper I have let the bread and cup pass me by, because I remembered the temper I lost this week, the things I should not have looked at, the resentment and coldness in my heart, and felt unworthy. Paul says, "Let a person examine himself, then, and so eat of the bread and drink of the cup." Self-examination is not meant to shut me out, but to bring all of this to the cross: to confess my sin; where I can be reconciled with those I have wronged, to seek it, and where I cannot yet, to entrust it to the Lord; and then to reach out my hand and receive. The Lord Jesus instituted this bread and cup on the night he was betrayed, the night all his disciples would desert him and Peter would deny him three times; yet he still said, "This is my body which is for you." I can come to the Supper not because I did well enough this week, but because his body has been given for me and his blood poured out for me. Or perhaps I am the one who usually eats alone at Sunday lunch, with no one making room for me; but at his own table the Lord says, "I have earnestly desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer" (Luke 22:15). Having received such grace, I can also invite another brother or sister who eats alone to sit at my table. Next time I come to the Supper, can I stop pulling my hand back, and trust that the Lord himself has set this table for me, and that one day I will drink it new with him in my Father's kingdom (Matt 26:29)?

entries.title: 你们就是基督的身子：恩赐原有分别，圣灵却是一位
entries.title_en: You Are the Body of Christ: Varieties of Gifts, but the Same Spirit

verse_parts.text: 你们就是基督的身子，并且各自作肢体。

entries.verse_text: 你们就是基督的身子，并且各自作肢体。
entries.content:
本章脉络

第十二至十四章讨论「属灵的恩赐」（林前12:1），特别是说方言和说预言的问题。第十二章奠定基础，分三段。认耶稣为主（1-3节）：辨别是不是出于圣灵，标准不是现象多么奇妙，而是承认「耶稣是主」。同一位圣灵，许多恩赐（4-11节）：「恩赐原有分别，圣灵却是一位」，「圣灵显在各人身上，是叫人得益处」。一个身体，许多肢体（12-31节）：「你们就是基督的身子，并且各自作肢体」；没有一个肢体可以说自己「不属乎身子」，也没有一个肢体可以说「我用不着你」。

这一章的中心是27节：教会不是一群各自追求恩赐的人，而是基督的身体。恩赐的目的，是叫整个身体得益处；第十三章随即指出那「最妙的道」，就是爱。

深读 12:1-3 认耶稣为主

1. 从哑巴偶像到圣灵。 「弟兄们，论到属灵的恩赐，我不愿意你们不明白。你们作外邦人的时候，随事被牵引，受迷惑，去服事那哑巴偶像，这是你们知道的。」（林前12:1-2）哥林多人从前拜偶像的时候，可能也有过出神、狂喜之类的宗教经验。保罗提醒他们：不是一切奇妙的灵性经验都出于神。

2. 「耶稣是主」。 「所以我告诉你们，被神的灵感动的，没有说『耶稣是可咒诅』的；若不是被圣灵感动的，也没有能说『耶稣是主』的。」（林前12:3）「耶稣是可咒诅」是什么情形，学者有不同的猜测；但保罗的重点是清楚的：圣灵的工作，总是叫人尊耶稣为主。这不是说任何人口里说了这几个字，就证明有圣灵；而是说，一个人真心承认耶稣是他的主，本身就是圣灵的工作。每一个真信徒，都已经有圣灵（参罗8:9）。

要点：辨别属灵恩赐的标准，不是现象多么奇妙，而是是否高举耶稣为主。每一个真心承认耶稣是主的人，都是被圣灵感动的。
深读 12:4-11 同一位圣灵，许多恩赐

1. 三位一体的神。 「恩赐原有分别，圣灵却是一位。职事也有分别，主却是一位。功用也有分别，神却是一位，在众人里面运行一切的事。」（林前12:4-6）圣灵、主（耶稣）、神（父），三位一同在教会中工作。教会中恩赐多样又彼此合一，正反映出三一神的合一与丰富：恩赐不同，却出于同一位神。

2. 叫人得益处。 「圣灵显在各人身上，是叫人得益处。」（林前12:7）这里有两个重点：第一，「各人」都有圣灵的显现，没有一个信徒是没有恩赐的；第二，恩赐的目的是「叫人得益处」，原文是为了共同的益处，不是为了显出自己属灵。

3. 恩赐的清单。 8-10节列出了九种恩赐：智慧的言语、知识的言语、信心、医病、行异能、作先知、辨别诸灵、说方言、翻方言。这不是全部的恩赐。比较罗12:6-8、弗4:11和彼前4:10-11，就知道圣经中还有教导、劝化、施舍、治理、怜悯、传福音、牧养等等。

4. 随己意分给各人。 「这一切都是这位圣灵所运行、随己意分给各人的。」（林前12:11）恩赐不是我们靠努力赚来的，也不是用来比较的，而是圣灵按着自己的主权白白分给的。

5. 恩赐今天还有吗？ 关于说方言、说预言、医病这一类恩赐今天是否仍然存在，福音派中有两种主要看法： - 终止论：许多学者，特别是在改革宗传统中（如华腓德〔B. B. Warfield〕、加芬〔Richard Gaffin〕），认为这些恩赐主要是为使徒时代立定根基（弗2:20），在使徒时代结束、根基立定以后就已经停止；神今天仍然按着他的旨意医治人、垂听祷告，但不再藉着这样的恩赐给人新的启示。 - 延续论：另一些学者，包括一些改革宗学者（如古德恩、派博），认为新约没有说这些恩赐会在主再来以前停止（参林前13:8-10），所以今天仍然存在；但一切都要按圣经察验（林前14:29；帖前5:20-21），不能与圣经同等。

此外，古典五旬节派认为说方言是受圣灵洗的最初凭据；可是保罗在林前12:30问：「岂都是说方言的吗？」这个问题所期待的答案是「不是」。五旬节派的回应是：林前12:30讲的是在聚会中公开说方言的恩赐，与受灵洗时的方言不同；但大多数福音派学者认为，经文本身并没有作这样的区分。也有一些学者（如卡森）采取开放而谨慎的立场。华人教会中，这几种看法都有：有的教会认为非说方言不可，有的则对灵恩运动十分戒备，灵恩和非灵恩的教会彼此猜疑、互相论断的情形并不少见。若有人对我说，我不说方言，所以还没有圣灵，林前12:3和林前12:13告诉我：真心承认耶稣是主的人，都已经在一位圣灵里受洗，进了这身体；反过来，有不同经历的弟兄姊妹，也不该被看作异类。不论采取哪一种看法，第十二章的教导都一样适用：恩赐出于同一位圣灵，是为了造就整个身体，不是为了分辨谁比较属灵。

要点：每一个信徒都有圣灵所赐的恩赐，没有一种恩赐是为了显出自己。恩赐不同，却出于同一位神，为了叫众人得益处。
深读 12:12-26 一个身体，许多肢体

1. 基督也是这样。 「就如身子是一个，却有许多肢体；而且肢体虽多，仍是一个身子；基督也是这样。我们不拘是犹太人，是希腊人，是为奴的，是自主的，都从一位圣灵受洗，成了一个身体，饮于一位圣灵。」（林前12:12-13）保罗没有说教会也是这样，而是说「基督也是这样」：教会与基督联合，是他的身体。「都从一位圣灵受洗」，大多数福音派学者认为是指每一个信徒在信主时都经历的事；五旬节派则常常把「灵洗」理解为信主以后的另一次经历。保罗在这里强调的是「都」：没有一个信徒在这个身体以外。

2. 「不属乎身子」？ 「设若脚说：『我不是手，所以不属乎身子，』它不能因此就不属乎身子。」（林前12:15）这是对自卑的人说的。有人觉得自己的恩赐不显眼，不能讲道、不能领诗，就以为自己在教会中可有可无。保罗说：你属不属于这个身体，不是由你自己的感觉决定的，而是神「随自己的意思把肢体俱各安排在身上了」（林前12:18）。

3. 「我用不着你」。 「眼不能对手说：『我用不着你』；头也不能对脚说：『我用不着你。』」（林前12:21）这是对骄傲的人说的。有恩赐、有地位的人，很容易觉得别人可有可无。可是保罗说：「身上肢体人以为软弱的，更是不可少的。」（林前12:22）保罗说的是「人以为」软弱的：软弱常常在我们的眼光里，不在他们身上。年长的、患病的、残障的、不善言辞的弟兄姊妹，不只是教会照顾的对象，更是神放在身体里、有恩赐可以给出来的肢体；他们若进不了门、听不见、跟不上，缺欠的是整个身体。

4. 彼此相顾。 「免得身上分门别类，总要肢体彼此相顾。若一个肢体受苦，所有的肢体就一同受苦；若一个肢体得荣耀，所有的肢体就一同快乐。」（林前12:25-26）这正击中哥林多教会的问题：他们在领袖的事上分党（林前1:10-12），在主的晚餐上「彼此分门别类」（林前11:18）。在基督的身体里，别人的痛苦就是我的痛苦，别人的荣耀也是我的快乐；不是嫉妒，也不是冷漠。

要点：在基督的身体里，没有一个肢体是多余的，也没有一个肢体可以不需要别人。软弱的，更是不可少的。
深读 12:27-31 你们就是基督的身子

1. 各自作肢体。 「你们就是基督的身子，并且各自作肢体。」（林前12:27）这是全章的总结。「你们」是复数，是指整个教会；「各自」是说每一个人都在其中。

2. 第一是使徒。 「神在教会所设立的：第一是使徒，第二是先知，第三是教师，其次是行异能的，再次是得恩赐医病的，帮助人的，治理事的，说方言的。」（林前12:28）保罗列出的头三项，都是与神的话语有关的职事；说方言被列在最后，可能是因为哥林多人过分看重它，保罗有意把它放在后面。「帮助人的，治理事的」也在清单中：那些在幕后默默服事的人，同样是神在教会中「设立」的。

3. 岂都是？ 「岂都是使徒吗？岂都是先知吗？……岂都是说方言的吗？岂都是翻方言的吗？」（林前12:29-30）这些问题在原文中都期待「不是」的回答。神从来没有要每一个信徒都有同样的恩赐。

4. 更大的恩赐与最妙的道。 「你们要切切地求那更大的恩赐。我现今把最妙的道指示你们。」（林前12:31）「切切地求」大多数译本理解为命令，就是要追求那些更能造就人的恩赐（参林前14:1，5，12）；也有人理解为保罗在描述哥林多人的现况：你们正热切地追求那些看起来更大的恩赐。无论哪一种，保罗接着要指出的，都比任何恩赐更美：那就是爱（13章）。

要点：神在教会中设立了不同的恩赐，没有人拥有全部，也没有人一无所有。比一切恩赐更美的，是爱。
默想

默想： 「设若脚说：『我不是手，所以不属乎身子，』它不能因此就不属乎身子。」我从小学到的是：有用的人才有价值。考试要考好，工作要有成就，在教会里也要有拿得出手的恩赐。所以，当我不会讲道、不会弹琴、不会带小组，或者年纪大了、身体不好、刚刚失业，觉得什么都给不了的时候，我就以为自己在教会里可有可无。也许我也曾经是那只「眼」，心里对某些弟兄姊妹说：「我用不着你」；其实我看不起别人，常常是因为我需要觉得自己重要。保罗说，我属于基督的身体，不是因为我有用，而是因为我已经在一位圣灵里「受洗，成了一个身体」，是神「随自己的意思」把我安排在这里（林前12:13，18）。如果我曾经看不起别人，我可以向主认罪，他必赦免我；他也差我去告诉一位看起来软弱的弟兄姊妹：「这个家需要你。」我们的主耶稣「因软弱被钉在十字架上」（林后13:4），他最荣耀的工作，正是在最软弱的时候完成的。今天，我能不能相信：那位为我软弱、为我死的主，正是「把加倍的体面给那有缺欠的肢体」的神（林前12:24）；在他的身体里，我不是可有可无的？
entries.content_en:
The Shape of the Chapter

Chapters 12–14 address "spiritual gifts" (1 Corinthians 12:1), especially tongues and prophecy. Chapter 12 lays the foundation, in three parts. Confessing Jesus as Lord (vv. 1–3): the test of what comes from the Spirit is not how wonderful an experience seems, but the confession "Jesus is Lord." One Spirit, many gifts (vv. 4–11): "there are varieties of gifts, but the same Spirit," and "to each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good." One body, many members (vv. 12–31): "you are the body of Christ and individually members of it"; no member may say "I do not belong to the body," and none may say "I have no need of you."

The center of the chapter is verse 27: the church is not a crowd of individuals each pursuing gifts, but the body of Christ. The purpose of the gifts is the good of the whole body, and chapter 13 then shows the "still more excellent way," which is love.

Going Deeper: 12:1–3 Confessing Jesus as Lord

1. From mute idols to the Spirit. "Now concerning spiritual gifts, brothers, I do not want you to be uninformed. You know that when you were pagans you were led astray to mute idols, however you were led" (1 Corinthians 12:1–2). When the Corinthians worshiped idols, they may well have had religious experiences such as trance or ecstasy. Paul reminds them that not every remarkable spiritual experience comes from God.

2. "Jesus is Lord." "Therefore I want you to understand that no one speaking in the Spirit of God ever says 'Jesus is accursed!' and no one can say 'Jesus is Lord' except in the Holy Spirit" (1 Corinthians 12:3). Scholars offer different guesses about the situation behind "Jesus is accursed," but Paul's point is clear: the Spirit's work always leads people to honor Jesus as Lord. This doesn't mean anyone who pronounces the words thereby proves he has the Spirit; it means that genuinely confessing Jesus as one's Lord is itself the Spirit's work. Every true believer already has the Spirit (cf. Rom 8:9).

The point: The test of spiritual gifts is not how remarkable they appear, but whether they exalt Jesus as Lord. Everyone who truly confesses Jesus as Lord does so by the Holy Spirit.
Going Deeper: 12:4–11 One Spirit, Many Gifts

1. The triune God. "Now there are varieties of gifts, but the same Spirit; and there are varieties of service, but the same Lord; and there are varieties of activities, but it is the same God who empowers them all in everyone" (1 Corinthians 12:4–6). The Spirit, the Lord (Jesus) and God (the Father) work together in the church. The church's variety reflects the unity and richness of the triune God: the gifts differ, but they come from the one God.

2. For the common good. "To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good" (1 Corinthians 12:7). There are two points here. First, "to each": every believer has a manifestation of the Spirit; no believer is without a gift. Second, the purpose of the gifts is "the common good," not displaying one's own spirituality.

3. The list of gifts. Verses 8–10 list nine gifts: the utterance of wisdom, the utterance of knowledge, faith, healing, miracles, prophecy, distinguishing between spirits, tongues and the interpretation of tongues. This is not every gift. Comparing Romans 12:6–8, Ephesians 4:11 and 1 Peter 4:10–11 shows that Scripture also names teaching, exhortation, giving, leading, mercy, evangelism, shepherding and more.

4. As he wills. "All these are empowered by one and the same Spirit, who apportions to each one individually as he wills" (1 Corinthians 12:11). Gifts are not earned by effort, nor meant for comparison; the Spirit gives them freely by his own sovereign choice.

5. Do these gifts continue today? Evangelicals hold two main views on whether gifts such as tongues, prophecy and healing continue today: - Cessationism: many scholars, especially in the Reformed tradition (e.g. B. B. Warfield, Richard Gaffin), hold that these gifts served mainly to lay the foundation in the apostolic age (Eph 2:20) and ceased once that apostolic foundation was laid; God still heals and answers prayer according to his will today, but no longer gives new revelation through such gifts. - Continuationism: other scholars, including some in the Reformed tradition (e.g. Wayne Grudem, John Piper), hold that the New Testament does not say these gifts will cease before the Lord returns (cf. 1 Corinthians 13:8–10), so they continue today; but everything must be tested by Scripture (1 Corinthians 14:29; 1 Thess 5:20–21) and can never stand on a level with it.

In addition, classical Pentecostals hold that speaking in tongues is the initial evidence of baptism in the Spirit; yet in 1 Corinthians 12:30 Paul asks, "Do all speak with tongues?", a question that expects the answer "No." Pentecostals reply that 1 Corinthians 12:30 concerns the gift of tongues exercised in the assembly, distinct from tongues as the sign of Spirit baptism; most evangelical scholars find no such distinction in the text. Some (e.g. D. A. Carson) take an "open but cautious" position. All these views are found in Chinese churches: some insist that one must speak in tongues, others are deeply wary of the charismatic movement, and charismatic and non-charismatic churches often regard each other with suspicion and judgment. If someone has told me that because I don't speak in tongues I lack the Spirit, 1 Corinthians 12:3 and 1 Corinthians 12:13 say that everyone who truly confesses Jesus as Lord has been baptized in the one Spirit into the body; and brothers and sisters with different experiences should not be treated as outsiders. Whichever view one holds, the teaching of chapter 12 applies equally: the gifts come from one Spirit to build up the whole body, not to sort out who is more spiritual.

The point: Every believer has a gift from the Spirit, and no gift is for showing off. The gifts differ, but they come from the one God for the good of all.
Going Deeper: 12:12–26 One Body, Many Members

1. So it is with Christ. "For just as the body is one and has many members, and all the members of the body, though many, are one body, so it is with Christ. For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body, Jews or Greeks, slaves or free, and all were made to drink of one Spirit" (1 Corinthians 12:12–13). Paul doesn't say "so it is with the church," but "so it is with Christ": the church is united to Christ as his body. "In one Spirit we were all baptized" is taken by most evangelical scholars to describe what every believer experiences at conversion; Pentecostals often understand "Spirit baptism" as a further experience after conversion. Paul's emphasis here is on "all": no believer is outside this body.

2. "I do not belong to the body." "If the foot should say, 'Because I am not a hand, I do not belong to the body,' that would not make it any less a part of the body" (1 Corinthians 12:15). This is addressed to those who feel inferior. Some feel that their gifts are not visible: they can't preach or lead worship, so they think they make no difference in the church. Paul says that whether you belong to the body isn't decided by your feelings; "God arranged the members in the body, each one of them, as he chose" (1 Corinthians 12:18).

3. "I have no need of you." "The eye cannot say to the hand, 'I have no need of you,' nor again the head to the feet, 'I have no need of you'" (1 Corinthians 12:21). This is addressed to the proud. People with gifts and standing can easily feel that others make no difference. But Paul says, "the parts of the body that seem to be weaker are indispensable" (1 Corinthians 12:22). Paul says the parts that seem weaker: the weakness is often in our eyes, not in them. Elderly, sick and disabled brothers and sisters, and those who are not good with words, are not only people for the church to care for; they are members God has placed in the body, with gifts to give. If they cannot get in the door, hear, or keep up, it is the whole body that is lacking.

4. Caring for one another. "That there may be no division in the body, but that the members may have the same care for one another. If one member suffers, all suffer together; if one member is honored, all rejoice together" (1 Corinthians 12:25–26). This speaks directly to the Corinthian church's problems: "divisions" over leaders (1 Corinthians 1:10–12) and at the Lord's Supper (1 Corinthians 11:18). In the body of Christ, another's pain is my pain, and another's honor is my joy: neither envy nor indifference.

The point: In the body of Christ no member is superfluous, and no member can do without the others. The weaker members are indispensable.
Going Deeper: 12:27–31 You Are the Body of Christ

1. Individually members. "Now you are the body of Christ and individually members of it" (1 Corinthians 12:27). This sums up the chapter. "You" is plural, meaning the whole church; "individually" means each person has a place in it.

2. First apostles. "And God has appointed in the church first apostles, second prophets, third teachers, then miracles, then gifts of healing, helping, administrating, and various kinds of tongues" (1 Corinthians 12:28). The first three are all ministries of God's word; tongues come last, perhaps deliberately, because the Corinthians prized them too highly. "Helping" and "administrating" are on the list too: those who serve quietly behind the scenes are equally "appointed" by God in the church.

3. Are all...? "Are all apostles? Are all prophets?... Do all speak with tongues? Do all interpret?" (1 Corinthians 12:29–30). In Greek each of these questions expects the answer "No." God never intended every believer to have the same gift.

4. Higher gifts and a more excellent way. "But earnestly desire the higher gifts. And I will show you a still more excellent way" (1 Corinthians 12:31). Most translations take "earnestly desire" as a command: pursue the gifts that build others up more (cf. 1 Corinthians 14:1, 5, 12). Others take it as Paul describing the Corinthians' present state: you are eagerly pursuing the gifts that look greater. Either way, what Paul goes on to show is better than any gift: love (ch. 13).

The point: God has appointed different gifts in the church; no one has them all, and no one has none. Better than every gift is love.
Meditation

Reflect: "If the foot should say, 'Because I am not a hand, I do not belong to the body,' that would not make it any less a part of the body." I learned young that only useful people are worth anything. I had to do well in exams, achieve at work, and have a gift at church I could point to. So when I can't preach, can't play an instrument, can't lead a small group, or I'm getting old, my health is poor, I've just lost my job and feel I have nothing to give, I assume I make no difference at church. Or perhaps I have been the "eye," saying in my heart to certain brothers and sisters, "I have no need of you"; and often I look down on others because I need to feel important. Paul says I belong to the body of Christ not because I am useful, but because in one Spirit I was "baptized into one body," and God has placed me here "as he chose" (1 Corinthians 12:13, 18). If I have looked down on others, I can confess it to the Lord, and he will forgive me; and he sends me to tell a brother or sister who seems weak, "This family needs you." Our Lord Jesus "was crucified in weakness" (2 Cor 13:4); his most glorious work was accomplished in his weakest hour. Today, can I believe that the Lord who became weak and died for me is the God who gives "greater honor to the part that lacked it" (1 Corinthians 12:24), and that in his body I am not dispensable?

entries.title: 如今常存的有信，有望，有爱：其中最大的是爱
entries.title_en: Faith, Hope and Love Abide: The Greatest of These Is Love

verse_parts.text: 如今常存的有信，有望，有爱这三样，其中最大的是爱。

entries.verse_text: 如今常存的有信，有望，有爱这三样，其中最大的是爱。
entries.content:
本章脉络

第十三章夹在讨论属灵恩赐的第十二章和第十四章中间，是保罗所说的「最妙的道」（林前12:31）。这一章分三段。没有爱，就算不得什么（1-3节）：说方言、作先知、有信心、舍己，若没有爱，都毫无益处。爱是什么（4-7节）：保罗用十五个动词描写爱，有些说爱做什么，有些说爱不做什么。爱是永不止息（8-13节）：恩赐都是暂时的、有限的，「等那完全的来到」就要归于无有；「如今常存的有信，有望，有爱这三样，其中最大的是爱」。

这一章常在婚礼上诵读，这样用并没有错；但保罗原是写给一个彼此嫉妒、自高自大、争夺恩赐的教会。每一句描写爱的话，都在照出哥林多人的问题，也照出我们的问题。

深读 13:1-3 没有爱

1. 鸣的锣，响的钹。 「我若能说万人的方言，并天使的话语，却没有爱，我就成了鸣的锣，响的钹一般。」（林前13:1）哥林多人最看重说方言。保罗说：就算能说天使的话语，若没有爱，也只是噪音，许多人认为这是指异教神庙里敲锣打钹的声音。

2. 算不得什么。 「我若有先知讲道之能，也明白各样的奥秘，各样的知识，而且有全备的信，叫我能够移山，却没有爱，我就算不得什么。」（林前13:2）保罗不是说这些恩赐不好（他在林前14:1还要人「切慕」），而是说：一个人可能有很大的恩赐，却在神面前「算不得什么」。

3. 舍己身叫人焚烧。 「我若将所有的周济穷人，又舍己身叫人焚烧，却没有爱，仍然与我无益。」（林前13:3）连最大的牺牲，也可能不是出于爱，而是出于骄傲。这节有一个抄本上的差异：和合本和英文标准译本的正文都作「焚烧」；但许多较早的抄本作「叫我可以夸口」（这两个希腊词只差一个字母），今天通行的希腊文本（NA28）采用后者。无论哪一种，意思都是：外表的舍己，不等于爱。

要点：恩赐、知识和牺牲本身都不能证明我们属灵；没有爱，一切都算不得什么。
深读 13:4-7 爱是什么

1. 爱是行动。 「爱是恒久忍耐，又有恩慈；爱是不嫉妒；爱是不自夸，不张狂，不做害羞的事，不求自己的益处，不轻易发怒，不计算人的恶，不喜欢不义，只喜欢真理；凡事包容，凡事相信，凡事盼望，凡事忍耐。」（林前13:4-7）在原文中，这些都是动词。保罗没有给爱下一个抽象的定义，而是描写爱怎样对待人。

2. 一面镜子。 这些描写几乎都对着哥林多人的问题： - 他们有「嫉妒、纷争」（林前3:3），爱却「不嫉妒」； - 他们「自高自大」（林前4:6；林前8:1），爱却「不张狂」； - 他们在主的晚餐上各吃各的，在法庭上彼此相告，爱却「不求自己的益处」（参林前10:24）。

这一段不只是一首美丽的诗，更是一面镜子。

3. 「凡事包容」不是纵容恶。 「凡事包容，凡事相信」不是说要相信一切谎言、容忍一切恶行。同一段经文说，爱「不喜欢不义，只喜欢真理」（林前13:6）。爱不会为了表面的和平，把罪掩盖起来；面对家庭暴力或虐待，爱的做法是揭露恶、保护受害人。受害人可以，也应当寻求保护，包括报警（罗13:4），不必为了「包容」而留在危险中；教会也不可以拿「凡事包容」作理由，要受害人沉默，或为了「家丑不可外扬」而遮掩。「凡事相信，凡事盼望」也不是说，施害的人一道歉，就要立刻相信他，恢复他的职分，或让他再接近受害人和孩子。「凡事包容」的意思是：爱愿意为人承担，不轻易放弃人，也不急着把人往坏处想。

4. 只有一位完全符合。 有人建议，读这段经文时，把「爱」换成自己的名字：「某某是恒久忍耐，又有恩慈……」读不了几句，我们就读不下去了。可是若换成「耶稣」，每一句都完全符合：他「爱世间属自己的人，就爱他们到底」（约13:1）。保罗在这里描写的是爱，而这样的爱只有在基督身上完全显明出来；然后才在那些被他爱、被他改变的人身上，开始显出来。我们能这样爱，是因为「不是我们爱神，乃是神爱我们，差他的儿子为我们的罪作了挽回祭，这就是爱了」（约一4:10）。

要点：爱不只是一种感觉，而是怎样对待人。只有基督完全活出了这样的爱；我们被他所爱，才能开始这样爱人。
深读 13:8-13 爱是永不止息

1. 恩赐终必止息。 「爱是永不止息。先知讲道之能终必归于无有；说方言之能终必停止；知识也终必归于无有。我们现在所知道的有限，先知所讲的也有限，等那完全的来到，这有限的必归于无有了。」（林前13:8-10）哥林多人以为恩赐最重要，保罗却说：恩赐都是暂时的，爱却永远长存。

2. 「那完全的」是什么？ 这里有几种主要理解： - 基督再来、我们面对面见主的时候：大多数解经家都这样理解，因为12节说「到那时就要面对面了」。持这种看法的人中，有延续论者（如古德恩），也有许多终止论者（如加芬），后者认为恩赐的止息要根据别的经文来判断，不是根据这一节。 - 新约正典的完成：有些终止论者（多见于时代论传统）认为，「完全的」与「有限的」启示（先知讲道、知识）相对，所以是指圣经全部写成。 - 教会的成熟：也有人根据11节「作孩子……成了人」，认为是指教会的成熟。

反对后两种看法的人指出，「面对面」和「全知道，如同主知道我一样」很难用来描写今天。

这与第十二章所说终止论和延续论的讨论相关；但不论哪一种看法，保罗的重点都是：今天我们所知道的都是有限的，惟有爱永远长存。

3. 对着镜子观看。 「我们如今仿佛对着镜子观看，模糊不清，到那时就要面对面了。我如今所知道的有限，到那时就全知道，如同主知道我一样。」（林前13:12）古代的镜子是用磨光的铜做的，哥林多正以出产铜器闻名。铜镜照出来的像，总不如面对面看得清楚。「模糊不清」原文是在谜中，许多人认为这是在呼应民12:8：神与摩西「面对面说话，乃是明说，不用谜语」。我们今天对神的认识是真实的，却是有限的；到那日，我们要「面对面」见他（参约一3:2）。最安慰人的是后半句：在我还不完全认识神的时候，神早已完全认识我（参林前8:3）。

4. 其中最大的是爱。 「如今常存的有信，有望，有爱这三样，其中最大的是爱。」（林前13:13）为什么爱最大？有人认为，到那日信要变成眼见（林后5:7），望要变成实现（罗8:24），爱却永不过去；也有人指出，保罗说这三样都「常存」，在永恒里我们仍要信靠神、仰望神。无论哪一种理解，爱最大，是因为「神就是爱」（约一4:16）：神不需要信，也不需要望，神却是爱。我们在天上要做的，就是永远爱神、爱人；今天在地上学习爱，就是在预备那永远的生活。

要点：恩赐会止息，知识是有限的，但爱永不止息。我们今天对神的认识模糊不清，神对我们的认识却是完全的。
默想

默想： 「爱是恒久忍耐，又有恩慈。」请想一个在我生活中最难爱的人：也许是一位常常挑剔我的长辈，一位得了失智症、天天重复同样问题的父母，一位让我失望的配偶，或者一个怎么说都不听的孩子。现在，把林前13:4-7读一遍，把「爱」换成我的名字，想着这个人：「某某是恒久忍耐……不轻易发怒，不计算人的恶……」我能读到哪一句？也许不到第二句，我就要停下来，向主承认：我做不到。然后，请再读一遍，这次把「爱」换成「耶稣」，想着我自己：耶稣对我恒久忍耐，耶稣不计算我的恶，因为他已经在十字架上为我担当了（彼前2:24），耶稣凡事为我盼望。正当我还是罪人的时候，基督为我死（罗5:8）；他对我的忍耐，比我对任何人的忍耐都更长。今天我面对那个难爱的人，不是靠咬紧牙关，而是带着这样被爱的心，求圣灵在我里面结出「忍耐、恩慈」的果子（加5:22）。若这个人正在伤害我，爱也不是要我留在危险中；但无论如何，我可以先在主面前，领受他对我那「永不止息」的爱。
entries.content_en:
The Shape of the Chapter

Chapter 13 sits between chapters 12 and 14 on spiritual gifts; it is the "still more excellent way" (1 Corinthians 12:31). It has three parts. Without love, nothing (vv. 1–3): tongues, prophecy, faith and self-sacrifice gain nothing without love. What love is (vv. 4–7): Paul describes love with fifteen verbs, some saying what love does and some what it does not do. Love never ends (vv. 8–13): the gifts are temporary and partial and will pass away "when the perfect comes"; "So now faith, hope, and love abide, these three; but the greatest of these is love."

This chapter is often read at weddings, and that is not wrong; but Paul first wrote it to a church full of envy and arrogance, competing over spiritual gifts. Every line describing love exposes the Corinthians' problems, and ours.

Going Deeper: 13:1–3 Without Love

1. A noisy gong, a clanging cymbal. "If I speak in the tongues of men and of angels, but have not love, I am a noisy gong or a clanging cymbal" (1 Corinthians 13:1). The Corinthians prized tongues above all. Paul says that even speaking the language of angels without love is only noise; many think of the gongs and cymbals of pagan cults.

2. Nothing. "And if I have prophetic powers, and understand all mysteries and all knowledge, and if I have all faith, so as to remove mountains, but have not love, I am nothing" (1 Corinthians 13:2). Paul isn't saying these gifts are bad (in 1 Corinthians 14:1 he tells them to "earnestly desire" them); he is saying a person can have great gifts and still be "nothing" before God.

3. Delivering up my body to be burned. "If I give away all I have, and if I deliver up my body to be burned, but have not love, I gain nothing" (1 Corinthians 13:3). Even the greatest sacrifice can come from pride rather than love. There is a manuscript difference here: the CUV and ESV text read "burned"; but several of the earliest manuscripts read "that I may boast" (the two Greek words differ by one letter), and the standard Greek text today (NA28) prints that reading. Either way the point is that outward self-sacrifice is not the same as love.

The point: Gifts, knowledge and sacrifice cannot by themselves prove that we are spiritual; without love, all of it is nothing.
Going Deeper: 13:4–7 What Love Is

1. Love acts. "Love is patient and kind; love does not envy or boast; it is not arrogant or rude. It does not insist on its own way; it is not irritable or resentful; it does not rejoice at wrongdoing, but rejoices with the truth. Love bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things" (1 Corinthians 13:4–7). In Greek these are all verbs. Paul doesn't give love an abstract definition; he describes how love treats people.

2. A mirror. Nearly every line answers a Corinthian problem: - they had "jealousy and strife" (1 Corinthians 3:3), but love "does not envy"; - they were "puffed up" (1 Corinthians 4:6; 1 Corinthians 8:1), but love "is not arrogant"; - they ate their own meals at the Lord's Supper and sued each other in court, but love "does not insist on its own way" (cf. 1 Corinthians 10:24).

This passage is not only a beautiful poem; it is a mirror.

3. "Bears all things" does not excuse evil. "Bears all things, believes all things" does not mean believing every lie or tolerating every wrong. The same passage says love "does not rejoice at wrongdoing, but rejoices with the truth" (1 Corinthians 13:6). Love does not cover sin for the sake of surface peace; faced with domestic violence or abuse, love exposes the evil and protects the victim. Victims may, and should, seek protection, including from the police (Rom 13:4), and need not stay in danger in the name of "bearing all things"; nor may the church use "love bears all things" to silence victims or hide abuse to save face. Nor does "believes all things, hopes all things" mean taking an abuser's apology at face value, restoring him to office, or giving him access again to victims or children. "Bears all things" means that love is willing to carry burdens for others, does not give up on people easily, and is slow to think the worst.

4. Only one fits. Some suggest reading this passage with your own name in place of "love": "So-and-so is patient and kind..." We can't get far before we have to stop. But put "Jesus" in its place and every line fits perfectly: "having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end" (John 13:1). Paul is describing love, and this love has been perfectly displayed only in Christ; only then does it begin to appear in those whom he loves and changes. We can love like this because "in this is love, not that we have loved God but that he loved us and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins" (1 John 4:10).

The point: Love is not merely a feeling but a way of treating people. Only Christ has lived this love perfectly; loved by him, we can begin to love like this.
Going Deeper: 13:8–13 Love Never Ends

1. The gifts will cease. "Love never ends. As for prophecies, they will pass away; as for tongues, they will cease; as for knowledge, it will pass away. For we know in part and we prophesy in part, but when the perfect comes, the partial will pass away" (1 Corinthians 13:8–10). The Corinthians thought the gifts mattered most; Paul says the gifts are temporary, but love lasts forever.

2. What is "the perfect"? There are several main readings: - Christ's return, when we see the Lord face to face: most interpreters take it this way, because verse 12 says "then face to face." Those who hold this view include continuationists (e.g. Wayne Grudem) and many cessationists (e.g. Richard Gaffin), who hold that whether the gifts have ceased must be decided from other texts, not this one. - The completion of the New Testament canon: some cessationists (often in the dispensational tradition) argue that "the perfect" stands opposite the "partial" revelation of prophecy and knowledge, and so means the completed Scriptures. - The church's maturity: others, from verse 11's picture of child and adult, take it as the church's maturity.

Those who reject the last two views note that "face to face" and "know fully, even as I have been fully known" are hard to apply to the present age.

This connects with the cessationist and continuationist discussion in chapter 12; but on any view Paul's point is that all we know now is partial, and only love lasts forever.

3. Seeing in a mirror. "For now we see in a mirror dimly, but then face to face. Now I know in part; then I shall know fully, even as I have been fully known" (1 Corinthians 13:12). Ancient mirrors were made of polished bronze, and Corinth was famous for its bronze work. A mirror image is never as clear as seeing face to face. "Dimly" is literally "in a riddle," and many take it as an echo of Numbers 12:8, where God speaks with Moses "clearly, and not in riddles." Our knowledge of God today is real but partial; on that day we will see him "face to face" (cf. 1 John 3:2). The most comforting words are the last ones: while I do not yet fully know God, God already fully knows me (cf. 1 Corinthians 8:3).

4. The greatest of these is love. "So now faith, hope, and love abide, these three; but the greatest of these is love" (1 Corinthians 13:13). Why is love the greatest? Some say that on that day faith will become sight (2 Cor 5:7) and hope will be fulfilled (Rom 8:24), while love never passes away. Others note that Paul says all three "abide," since even in eternity we will go on trusting and hoping in God. Either way, love is greatest because "God is love" (1 John 4:16): God neither believes nor hopes, but he loves. What we will do in heaven forever is love God and love one another; learning to love on earth now is preparation for that eternal life.

The point: The gifts will cease and our knowledge is partial, but love never ends. Our knowledge of God today is dim, but his knowledge of us is complete.
Meditation

Reflect: "Love is patient and kind." Think of the person in my life who is hardest to love: perhaps an elder who constantly criticizes me, a parent with dementia who asks the same question all day, a spouse who has disappointed me, or a child who won't listen however I say it. Now read 1 Corinthians 13:4–7 with my own name in place of "love," thinking of this person: "So-and-so is patient... is not irritable or resentful..." How far can I read? Perhaps before the second line I have to stop and admit to the Lord: I can't do this. Then read it again, this time putting "Jesus" in place of "love," and thinking of myself: Jesus is patient with me, Jesus keeps no record of my wrongs, because he bore them on the cross (1 Pet 2:24), Jesus hopes all things for me. While I was still a sinner, Christ died for me (Rom 5:8); his patience with me is longer than my patience with anyone. Today I face that hard-to-love person not by gritting my teeth but with a heart that has been loved like this, asking the Spirit to bear in me the fruit of "patience, kindness" (Gal 5:22). If this person is harming me, love does not ask me to stay in danger; but whatever the case, I can first receive, before the Lord, his love for me that "never ends."

entries.verse_text: 弟兄们，这却怎么样呢？你们聚会的时候，各人或有诗歌，或有教训，或有启示，或有方言，或有翻出来的话，凡事都当造就人。
entries.content:
本章脉络

第十四章把第十二、十三章的原则，应用在哥林多教会的聚会上。这一章分三段。作先知讲道比说方言更能造就教会（1-19节）：「说方言的，是造就自己；作先知讲道的，乃是造就教会。」保罗宁可「用悟性说五句教导人的话，强如说万句方言」。为不信的人着想（20-25节）：若外人进来，听见众人说方言，会以为「你们癫狂了」；若听见先知讲道，就可能「将脸伏地，敬拜神」。聚会的次序（26-40节）：「凡事都当造就人」，说方言和作先知讲道都要轮流、有人翻出来或慎思明辨，因为「神不是叫人混乱，乃是叫人安静」。中间有一段关于「妇女在会中要闭口不言」的话（33-36节），是新约中较难解的经文之一。

这一章的中心是26节：「凡事都当造就人。」聚会的目的，不是让人显出自己的恩赐，而是让众人被建立。这正是第十三章所说的爱。

深读 14:1-19 造就教会

1. 追求爱，切慕恩赐。 「你们要追求爱，也要切慕属灵的恩赐，其中更要羡慕的，是作先知讲道。」（林前14:1）保罗先说「追求爱」，接着第十三章。他没有贬低恩赐，却把恩赐放在爱的底下：恩赐是爱的工具。

2. 先知讲道是什么？ 「但作先知讲道的，是对人说，要造就、安慰、劝勉人。」（林前14:3）新约中的「作先知讲道」（和合本常译作「讲道」，原文是说预言）是什么，有不同的理解： - 许多终止论者（如加芬）认为，这是神直接的启示，带着神自己的权威，属于使徒时代的根基（弗2:20）。 - 许多延续论者（如古德恩）认为，这是圣灵感动人说出的、对会众有帮助的话，权威低于圣经，所以「其余的就当慎思明辨」（林前14:29）。 - 也有人（如加尔文）认为，在今天，这恩赐主要表现在解释和应用圣经上。

不论哪一种理解，保罗的重点都是：作先知讲道是用人听得懂的话，叫人得造就、安慰、劝勉。

3. 说方言是什么？ 「那说方言的，原不是对人说，乃是对神说，因为没有人听出来。然而，他在心灵里却是讲说各样的奥秘。」（林前14:2）方言是什么，也有不同的看法：有人认为是说话的人没有学过的外国语言，像五旬节那天一样（徒2:6-8）；也有人认为是一种不属于人间语言的祷告和赞美（参林前13:1「天使的话语」）。保罗承认说方言有价值：「说方言的，是造就自己」（林前14:4），他自己「说方言比你们众人还多」（林前14:18）。但在聚会中，没有翻出来的方言不能造就别人。

4. 用灵，也用悟性。 「我要用灵祷告，也要用悟性祷告；我要用灵歌唱，也要用悟性歌唱。不然，你用灵祝谢，那在座不通方言的人，既然不明白你的话，怎能在你感谢的时候说『阿们』呢？」（林前14:15-16）敬拜不只是情感的经验，也需要头脑明白。别人要能跟着说「阿们」，才算是一同敬拜。

5. 五句与万句。 「但在教会中，宁可用悟性说五句教导人的话，强如说万句方言。」（林前14:19）这句话对今天的教会仍然适用：讲台上说得多么动人、用了多少术语，不如几句让人听得懂、能带回家的话。

要点：聚会中的恩赐，要用人听得懂的方式，造就、安慰、劝勉别人。五句造就人的话，强如一万句只造就自己的话。
深读 14:20-25 为不信的人着想

1. 在心志上作大人。 「弟兄们，在心志上不要作小孩子。然而，在恶事上要作婴孩，在心志上总要作大人。」（林前14:20）哥林多人追求方言，像小孩子追求新奇的玩具。保罗要他们在思想上成熟。

2. 方言是给不信的人的记号。 「律法上记着：主说：我要用外邦人的舌头和外邦人的嘴唇向这百姓说话；虽然如此，他们还是不听从我。这样看来，说方言不是为信的人作证据，乃是为不信的人。」（林前14:21-22）保罗引用赛28:11-12：以色列人不肯听先知的话，神就让他们听见亚述人听不懂的语言，这是审判的记号。这段经文很难解，常见的理解是：在聚会中，听不懂的方言对不信的人来说，不会带来悔改，只会成为他们不信的记号，让他们觉得「你们癫狂了」（林前14:23）。

3. 「神真是在你们中间了」。 「若都作先知讲道，偶然有不信的，或是不通方言的人进来，就被众人劝醒，被众人审明，他心里的隐情显露出来，就必将脸伏地，敬拜神，说：『神真是在你们中间了。』」（林前14:24-25）这是聚会最好的结果：一个外人进来，不是被奇怪的现象吓走，而是听见神的话，被神光照，认罪悔改，敬拜神。

要点：聚会要考虑到不信的人和新来的人。最好的聚会，是让外人听见神的话，被光照，敬拜神。
深读 14:26-40 聚会的次序

1. 凡事都当造就人。 「弟兄们，这却怎么样呢？你们聚会的时候，各人或有诗歌，或有教训，或有启示，或有方言，或有翻出来的话，凡事都当造就人。」（林前14:26）这里看见早期教会的聚会，是许多人参与的。

2. 次序。 说方言的「只好两个人，至多三个人，且要轮流着说，也要一个人翻出来。若没有人翻，就当在会中闭口」；作先知讲道的「只好两个人或是三个人，其余的就当慎思明辨」（林前14:27-29）。「先知的灵原是顺服先知的；因为神不是叫人混乱，乃是叫人安静。」（林前14:32-33）圣灵的工作不会叫人失控，属灵的人可以安静、等候、轮流。「安静」原文是平安。

3. 「妇女在会中要闭口不言」。 「妇女在会中要闭口不言，像在圣徒的众教会一样，因为不准她们说话。她们总要顺服，正如律法所说的。她们若要学什么，可以在家里问自己的丈夫，因为妇女在会中说话原是可耻的。」（林前14:34-35）大多数解经家认为，这段话不能理解为妇女在聚会中完全不可以开口，因为保罗在林前11:5已经提到妇女在聚会中祷告、说预言；所以这里的「闭口」是指某种特定的说话。主要有以下几种理解： - 不参与评断先知讲道：许多主张男女角色有别的学者（如卡森、古德恩）认为，这段话紧接在29节「其余的就当慎思明辨」之后，指的是妇女不在会众面前公开评断先知的话，因为这涉及教导的权柄（参提前2:12）。 - 不在聚会中插嘴发问：许多学者，特别是平等派（如克雷格·基纳〔Craig Keener〕），认为，当时的妇女大多没有受过教育，可能在聚会中大声发问、打断讲话，所以保罗说「可以在家里问自己的丈夫」；这是为了聚会的秩序，不是一条永远禁止妇女说话的命令。 - 后来加进去的经文：也有一些学者，多为平等派（如戈登·费依），认为这两节可能是后来抄写的人加进去的，因为在少数西方抄本中，这两节被放在第40节之后；他们也认为这两节与林前11:5和上下文不协调。但现存的抄本没有一份缺少这两节，今天通行的希腊文本（NA28）和大多数福音派解经家都认为这是保罗原来的话。

「正如律法所说的」也不容易理解，因为旧约没有一节经文直接这样说。保罗在林前14:21把以赛亚书也称为「律法」，可见「律法」可以泛指旧约。有人认为是指创世记第二章的创造次序（参林前11:8-9；提前2:13），也有人认为是指创3:16，或泛指旧约的原则。华人教会在这件事上的做法也不一样：有的教会有女传道人讲道、教导，有的教会讲台只由弟兄负责，姊妹仍然祷告、作见证，也教导妇女和孩子。无论采取哪一种做法，都要记得：神的灵「浇灌凡有血气的」，「你们的儿女要说预言」（珥2:28；彼得在五旬节宣告这应许已经应验，徒2:17-18；参徒21:9），姊妹的恩赐是神给教会的礼物，不可轻看。

4. 主的命令。 「若有人以为自己是先知，或是属灵的，就该知道，我所写给你们的是主的命令。」（林前14:37）保罗所写的，不只是他个人的意见，而是主的命令。

5. 不要禁止，也要规矩。 「所以我弟兄们，你们要切慕作先知讲道，也不要禁止说方言。凡事都要规规矩矩地按着次序行。」（林前14:39-40）这一句平衡了两边：不要因为怕混乱就禁止圣灵的恩赐；也不要因为追求恩赐，就让聚会失去次序。

要点：圣灵不是叫人混乱，乃是叫人平安。聚会中的一切，都要规规矩矩、按着次序，好叫众人得造就。
默想

默想： 「作先知讲道的，是对人说，要造就、安慰、劝勉人。」请回想一句曾经扶持过我的话：也许是在我最灰心的时候，一位长辈拍拍我的肩膀说：「神没有忘记你」；也许是小组里一位弟兄姊妹为我祷告时说的一句经文；也许只是一条短信。那几句话不长，却在我心里留了很多年。保罗说，在教会里，「宁可用悟性说五句教导人的话，强如说万句方言」。我常常以为，造就人是牧师和讲员的事；可是保罗说「各人或有诗歌，或有教训」，每一个人都可以说几句造就人的话；即使我没有说预言的恩赐，保罗给先知讲道定下的目标，就是造就人，也是每个信徒说话的目标（弗4:29；帖前5:11）。我也会想起，我说过的一些话，不是造就人，而是伤人，甚至在教会里成了让人灰心的原因。今天，我能不能求主，把一个人放在我心里，让别人从前对我说过的那种话，现在借着我，说给他听？若我曾用话语伤了人，也可以先去认错。可是我能说出造就人的话，不是因为我口才好，而是因为我先听见了这样的话：神在这末世藉着他的儿子向我们说话（来1:2），他对我说的，不是定罪，而是「你的罪赦了」（可2:5）。这句话，就是我一切话语的源头。
entries.content_en:
The Shape of the Chapter

Chapter 14 applies the principles of chapters 12 and 13 to the Corinthian church's gatherings. It has three parts. Prophecy builds the church more than tongues (vv. 1–19): "The one who speaks in a tongue builds up himself, but the one who prophesies builds up the church." Paul "would rather speak five words with my mind in order to instruct others, than ten thousand words in a tongue." Thinking of unbelievers (vv. 20–25): if outsiders come in and hear everyone speaking in tongues, they will say "you are out of your minds"; if they hear prophecy, they may fall "on his face" and "worship God." Order in the gathering (vv. 26–40): "Let all things be done for building up"; tongues and prophecy should take turns, with interpretation or weighing, because "God is not a God of confusion but of peace." In the middle is a passage on women keeping "silent in the churches" (vv. 33–36), among the harder texts in the New Testament.

The center of the chapter is verse 26: "Let all things be done for building up." The purpose of the gathering is not for people to display their gifts, but for everyone to be built up. This is the love of chapter 13.

Going Deeper: 14:1–19 Building Up the Church

1. Pursue love, desire the gifts. "Pursue love, and earnestly desire the spiritual gifts, especially that you may prophesy" (1 Corinthians 14:1). Paul begins with "pursue love," continuing chapter 13. He doesn't belittle the gifts, but he puts them under love: gifts are tools of love.

2. What is prophecy? "On the other hand, the one who prophesies speaks to people for their upbuilding and encouragement and consolation" (1 Corinthians 14:3). What New Testament prophecy is has been understood in different ways: - Many cessationists (e.g. Richard Gaffin) hold that it was direct revelation from God, carrying God's own authority, belonging to the foundation laid in the apostolic age (Eph 2:20). - Many continuationists (e.g. Wayne Grudem) hold that it is Spirit-prompted speech that helps the congregation, with less authority than Scripture, which is why "the others weigh what is said" (1 Corinthians 14:29). - Others (e.g. Calvin) hold that today this gift is expressed mainly in explaining and applying Scripture.

On any view, Paul's point is that prophecy uses words people can understand, for their upbuilding, encouragement and consolation.

3. What are tongues? "For one who speaks in a tongue speaks not to men but to God; for no one understands him, but he utters mysteries in the Spirit" (1 Corinthians 14:2). Views differ on what tongues are. Some take them to be foreign languages the speaker had never learned, as at Pentecost (Acts 2:6–8); others take them to be prayer and praise not in any human language (cf. 1 Corinthians 13:1, "the tongues of men and of angels"). Paul grants that tongues have value: "The one who speaks in a tongue builds up himself" (1 Corinthians 14:4), and he himself speaks "in tongues more than all of you" (1 Corinthians 14:18). But in the gathering, uninterpreted tongues cannot build others up.

4. With the spirit and with the mind. "I will pray with my spirit, but I will pray with my mind also; I will sing praise with my spirit, but I will sing with my mind also. Otherwise, if you give thanks with your spirit, how can anyone in the position of an outsider say 'Amen' to your thanksgiving when he does not know what you are saying?" (1 Corinthians 14:15–16). Worship is not only an emotional experience; it also needs the mind to understand. Others must be able to say "Amen" for it to be shared worship.

5. Five words and ten thousand. "Nevertheless, in church I would rather speak five words with my mind in order to instruct others, than ten thousand words in a tongue" (1 Corinthians 14:19). This still applies to the church today: however moving a sermon is, however much specialized vocabulary it uses, a few words people can understand and take home are worth more.

The point: Gifts in the gathering are to be used in ways others can understand, for their upbuilding, encouragement and consolation. Five words that build others up are better than ten thousand that build up only oneself.
Going Deeper: 14:20–25 Thinking of Unbelievers

1. Mature in thinking. "Brothers, do not be children in your thinking. Be infants in evil, but in your thinking be mature" (1 Corinthians 14:20). The Corinthians chased tongues like children chasing a new toy. Paul wants them to mature in their thinking.

2. Tongues as a sign for unbelievers. "In the Law it is written, 'By people of strange tongues and by the lips of foreigners will I speak to this people, and even then they will not listen to me, says the Lord.' Thus tongues are a sign not for believers but for unbelievers" (1 Corinthians 14:21–22). Paul cites Isaiah 28:11–12: when Israel would not listen to the prophets, God made them hear the unintelligible language of the Assyrians, a sign of judgment. The passage is difficult; a common reading is that in the gathering, unintelligible tongues bring unbelievers not to repentance but to a sign of their unbelief, leaving them to say "you are out of your minds" (1 Corinthians 14:23).

3. "God is really among you." "But if all prophesy, and an unbeliever or outsider enters, he is convicted by all, he is called to account by all, the secrets of his heart are disclosed, and so, falling on his face, he will worship God and declare that God is really among you" (1 Corinthians 14:24–25). This is the best outcome of a gathering: an outsider comes in and, rather than being driven away by strange phenomena, hears God's word, is searched by God, confesses and repents, and worships God.

The point: Our gatherings must keep unbelievers and newcomers in mind. The best gathering is one where an outsider hears God's word, is searched by it and worships God.
Going Deeper: 14:26–40 Order in the Gathering

1. All things for building up. "What then, brothers? When you come together, each one has a hymn, a lesson, a revelation, a tongue, or an interpretation. Let all things be done for building up" (1 Corinthians 14:26). Here we see that the early church's gatherings involved many participants.

2. Order. For tongues, "let there be only two or at most three, and each in turn, and let someone interpret. But if there is no one to interpret, let each of them keep silent in church"; for prophecy, "let two or three prophets speak, and let the others weigh what is said" (1 Corinthians 14:27–29). "The spirits of prophets are subject to prophets. For God is not a God of confusion but of peace" (1 Corinthians 14:32–33). The Spirit's work does not make people lose control; spiritual people can be quiet, wait and take turns.

3. "The women should keep silent in the churches." "The women should keep silent in the churches. For they are not permitted to speak, but should be in submission, as the Law also says. If there is anything they desire to learn, let them ask their husbands at home. For it is shameful for a woman to speak in church" (1 Corinthians 14:34–35). Most interpreters conclude that this cannot mean women may never speak at all in the gathering, since in 1 Corinthians 11:5 Paul has already mentioned women praying and prophesying there; so the "silence" here concerns a particular kind of speech. The main readings are these: - Not taking part in weighing prophecies: many complementarian scholars (e.g. D. A. Carson, Wayne Grudem) note that this follows directly on verse 29, "let the others weigh what is said," and take it to mean that women should not publicly judge the prophets' words before the congregation, since that involves the authority to teach (cf. 1 Tim 2:12). - Not interrupting with questions: many scholars, especially egalitarians (e.g. Craig Keener), hold that most women then had little education and may have been calling out questions and interrupting, so Paul says "let them ask their husbands at home"; this is for the order of the gathering, not a permanent command forbidding women to speak. - A later addition: some scholars, mostly egalitarian (e.g. Gordon Fee), think these two verses may have been added later by a copyist, because in a few Western manuscripts they appear after verse 40; they also argue the verses fit poorly with 1 Corinthians 11:5 and the flow from verse 33 to verse 36. But no extant manuscript lacks them, and the standard Greek text (NA28) and most evangelical commentators retain them as Paul's own words.

"As the Law also says" is not easy either, since no Old Testament verse says this directly. In 1 Corinthians 14:21 Paul calls Isaiah "the Law," so the word can refer to the Old Testament generally. Some take it as the creation order of Genesis 2 (cf. 1 Corinthians 11:8–9; 1 Tim 2:13), others as Genesis 3:16, others as a general Old Testament principle. Chinese churches differ in practice: some have women pastors who preach and teach, others reserve the pulpit for men while sisters still pray, testify, and teach women and children. Whatever the practice, we must remember that God pours out his Spirit "on all flesh," and "your sons and your daughters shall prophesy" (Joel 2:28, which Peter declared fulfilled at Pentecost, Acts 2:17–18; cf. Acts 21:9); sisters' gifts are God's gift to the church and must not be despised.

4. A command of the Lord. "If anyone thinks that he is a prophet, or spiritual, he should acknowledge that the things I am writing to you are a command of the Lord" (1 Corinthians 14:37). What Paul writes is not merely his personal opinion but the Lord's command.

5. Do not forbid, and keep order. "So, my brothers, earnestly desire to prophesy, and do not forbid speaking in tongues. But all things should be done decently and in order" (1 Corinthians 14:39–40). This sentence balances both sides: don't forbid the Spirit's gifts out of fear of disorder, and don't let the gathering lose its order in pursuit of gifts.

The point: The Spirit brings not confusion but peace. Everything in the gathering should be done decently and in order, so that all are built up.
Meditation

Reflect: "The one who prophesies speaks to people for their upbuilding and encouragement and consolation." Recall a few words that once held me up: perhaps when I was most discouraged, an older believer patted my shoulder and said, "God has not forgotten you"; perhaps a verse a brother or sister prayed over me in small group; perhaps just a short text message. Those words were few, but they stayed with me for years. Paul says that in church he "would rather speak five words with my mind in order to instruct others, than ten thousand words in a tongue." I often think building others up is the work of pastors and speakers; but Paul says "each one has a hymn, a lesson," and everyone can speak a few words that build others up; even if I do not prophesy, the aim Paul gives prophecy, upbuilding, is the aim of every believer's speech (Eph 4:29; 1 Thess 5:11). I also remember words I have spoken that did not build up but wounded, words that even became a reason someone lost heart at church. Today, can I ask the Lord to lay one person on my heart, and let the kind of words someone once spoke to me now be spoken through me to them? If my words have wounded someone, I can first go and own it. Yet I can speak words that build up not because I am eloquent, but because I first heard words like these: in these last days God has spoken to us by his Son (Heb 1:2), and what he says to me is not condemnation but "your sins are forgiven" (Mark 2:5). That word is the source of every word I speak.
